item.title: SALES: The ‘Venice of Poland’ is the underrated and affordable festive break to know about this winter
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
With Christmas just around the corner, the time to start planning a festive getaway is now. From the traditional markets of Germany to the popular Christmas markets of Austria and Scandinavia, Europe has no shortage of destinations that go all out for the season. But if you're looking for somewhere a little less obvious (and more affordable), one Polish city might be worth adding to your list. Wrocław, in southwestern Poland, has come out on top in a new Christmas market ranking by Sainsbury's Travel Money, which compared destinations across 10 countries based on factors including size, tradition, prestige and value for money. Nicknamed the 'Venice of Poland' thanks to its waterways and around 100 bridges, the medieval city is particularly appealing to travellers hoping to enjoy a festive break without spending a fortune. According to the research, a meal for two costs around £38, a local draught beer £3.07 and a night in a mid-range hotel £49, bringing the combined total to approximately £90. The city's Christmas market takes over its historic Market Square, where vintage carousels and a huge fairytale house are among the attractions. Visitors can sip mulled wine from distinctive boot-shaped mugs and sample Polish specialities such as oscypek, a grilled mountain cheese typically served with cranberries. Another reason to consider Wrocław? Its Christmas market stays open well into January, running from 20 November 2026 until 7 January 2027. And it seems British travellers are increasingly looking towards Central and Eastern Europe for their winter getaways. Sainsbury's Travel Money reported a 53 per cent increase in sales of Polish złoty last Christmas compared with the summer period, while sales of Czech koruna rose by 19 per cent. Simon Phillips, Managing Director at Fexco, which owns Sainsbury’s Travel Money, commented: “While you’ll find Christmas trees and cheer wherever you go, in some destinations you’ll need something you may rarely use in the UK – cash. Stalls in many European Christmas markets don’t accept card or digital payments, so make sure you take some local currency with you.” Wrocław wasn't the only destination to score highly in the ranking. Riga, Latvia's capital, came second, followed by Prague in Czechia. Budapest rounded out the top five alongside Sapporo in Japan. For anyone tempted by a festive escape, Wrocław is also served by direct flights from nine UK airports, according to Sainsbury's Travel Money. With its medieval Market Square, traditional Christmas market, affordable prices and a lovely festive atmosphere that rivals Europe's biggest capitals, this Polish town is worth considering for a winter city break – especially if you are looking for some Christmas magic.

item.title: REVIEW: Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Cutting corners in the right places
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Medion’s Erazer Defender 17 P10 condenses a formidable spec into a reasonably priced package. It’s clear that corners have been cut with the less-than-premium body and poor battery life, but ultimately the Erazer Defender 17 P10 focuses its efforts on what gamers want most, and it largely succeeds on that front. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10: Two-minute review The Erazer Defender 17 P10 is a large and powerful gaming laptop with a price tag one could consider ‘budget’ when judging it against its rivals. It doesn’t look particularly exciting or stylish. There are a few discreet elements that evoke a gaming focus, but otherwise the P10’s design is purely functional. It doesn’t employ the most premium of materials, either, though the whole unit is reassuringly solid, save for the keyboard, which flexes considerably when you use it. And while it’s hardly the most portable device, there are worse 17-inch gaming machines to carry around. One of the benefits of this large size, though, is the space available for ports. On the rear of the Erazer Defender 17 P10 there are power, HDMI, and Ethernet connections, as well as a USB-C port that supports DisplayPort 1.4. On the right is another USB-C port that also supports DisplayPort 1.4, as well as Power Delivery. Two USB-A ports are featured on both sides, too, and the left side also gets a headset jack. When it comes to the business of gaming, the Erazer Defender 17 P10 is very capable. It managed to run various AAA titles at very high frame rates — above 60fps in many cases — with demanding graphics settings applied. More impressive is its cooling, although the price paid for this is persistent, if innocuous, fan noise. Despite its unspectacular 1080p resolution and lack of OLED tech (although this is a rarity for gaming laptops at this price point), the display also impressed me. Its vibrancy shows off games and other content in all their glory, and while its resolution isn’t the sharpest, it’s sharp enough to provide sufficient fidelity across the 17-inch real estate. The keyboard is great to use for both gaming and typing, thanks to the snappy and low-traveling — yet tactile — keys. That aforementioned flexing feels a little strange at first, but it actually provides cushioning and dampening, helping to nullify the harshness of furious presses. The touchpad is equally capable, thanks to its smooth surface, responsiveness, and large surface area. The battery life is on par for what you would expect of a gaming laptop — which is to say it’s not great. It lasted five and a half hours in our movie playback test, which is 40 minutes better than what the Medion Erazer Major 16 X1 achieved, although less than half the time posted by the Asus V16, a much cheaper gaming laptop. This aspect aside, though, the Erazer Defender 17 P10 is a strong performer with a welcome price tag relative to its spec. You’ll have to settle for an unspectacular design and a poor battery life, but if you think these aspects are worth sacrificing for gaming prowess, then the Erazer Defender 17 P10 represents good value in the large gaming laptop sector. Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Price & availability - Starts from £1,649.99 (about $2,200 / AU$3,150) The P10 starts from £1,649.99 (about $2,200 / AU$3,150) and is available in the UK only. The base model features an Intel Core i9-14900HX, an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, 16GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage. The higher-spec model costs £1,899.97 (about $2,500 / AU$3,600), and gets an RTX 5070 and 32GB of RAM. This is a reasonable price when you compare the Erazer Defender 17 P10 to other gaming laptops of a similar spec and size. There are a few budget offerings that rival its value for money, though: one of them is another Erazer model, the Major 16 X1. This is more expensive than the top P10 model, but its spec is better across the board, with its Intel Core Ultra 9, RTX 5070 Ti, 32GB of RAM, and 2TB of storage, not to mention its much sharper — but inch smaller — 1600p display. There’s also the Asus V16 for bargain hunters to consider, which we rate as one of the best budget gaming laptop picks around. This is much cheaper than any Erazer Defender 17 P10 model, but you’ll have to settle for a 40-series RTX, and it too has a smaller 16-inch display. Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Specs Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Design & features While the materials employed aren’t the most premium, the unit is mostly solid, aside from the flexing on the keyboard. And I certainly welcomed the smoothness of the keyboard enclosure when resting my wrists on it. Thankfully, the keys are of a higher quality, featuring a subtle texturing and a fetching floating design. As always, I’m glad to see a full-size layout on a laptop, although I would expect nothing less from a 17-inch device. There are some useful Fn shortcuts on the Function row, and both they and all the other keys can be reprogrammed using the preinstalled Control Center utility software. Granted, this is limited to macro recording with the keys already on the board — far more spartan compared to the best gaming keyboard software — but it’s uncommon to see any such software for laptop keyboards. As you might expect from a 17-inch gaming laptop, the Erazer Defender 17 P10 isn’t exactly the most portable device in the world. However, it’s just about light and thin enough to stuff into a backpack. Another more positive expectation you may have from such a machine is a large number of ports, and thankfully the Erazer Defender 17 P10 meets this too. At the back, you’ll find the power adapter socket, flanked on both sides by an Ethernet port, an HDMI port, and a USB-C port that supports the DisplayPort 1.4 standard — practical locations for such connections. On the right are two USB ports: one type-A and the other type-C. The latter again supports the DisplayPort 1.4 standard, but with additional Power Delivery support. On the left is another USB-A port and a 3.5mm headset jack. All these side ports are all placed further forward than is typical, which might be a problem for those who don’t like cables protruding from the middle of their laptop. Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Performance - Fans are loud but provide great cooling The performance of the Erazer Defender 17 P10 is impressive. I managed to get 60-70fps when I played Cyberpunk 2077 on the Ray Tracing: Low preset, and it even did an admirable job of handling Ray Tracing: Ultra, giving me around 40 fps, although drops into the thirties and below occurred during more chaotic scenes. In order to handle this kind of intensity, the fans fire up at the slightest provocation when they’re set to the Performance mode. But while the noise is certainly noticeable and near-constant, I didn’t find its tone harsh. What’s more, they do a very admirable job of keeping the Erazer Defender 17 P10 cool at all times; no doubt this is also thanks to the large vents on the sides, back, and underneath, as well as the sheer size of the unit itself helping to dissipate heat. Content looks surprisingly sharp on the P10, given the large 17-inch real estate is only given a 1080p resolution to work with, although some loss in fidelity is apparent. It’s also pleasingly vibrant and has acceptable levels of contrast, despite lacking OLED technology. It can be reflective, especially when displaying darker scenes, but in the main the brightness levels are sufficient to maintain good visibility. Whether you’re gaming or working, the Erazer Defender 17 P10’s keyboard is up to the task. The keys are very light and snappy with a low travel, while at the same time providing good tactility. This makes them great for rapid yet controlled spamming, as well as typing. Their generous spacing also helps with the latter, and compensates for their oddly narrow form. That aforementioned flexing is a blessing, too, as it acts to cushion presses in the absence of dampening materials underneath the keys. I found this a little disconcerting at first, but after I adjusted, I found it to be a boon. When my fingers were on the WASD keys, I did find the space bar a little too short to use optimally with my thumb. This is a minor gripe, though, and mostly I found it comfortable to game in this position. The touchpad is also easy to use, thanks to its smooth surface and responsiveness, although there were times when taps failed to register. It’s also large enough to facilitate easy navigation, but can occasionally get in the way while typing; I found that initial contact with my palm would trigger it, but further contact after that would be blocked. Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Battery life As is the case with many large gaming laptops, the Erazer Defender 17 P10 has a short battery life. It lasted five and a half hours when I ran a movie on a continuous loop, which makes it more enduring than the Erazer Major 16 X1, but only by 40 minutes. However, it’s a lot shorter-lived than the Asus V16, which is something of an outlier in the sector and lasted close to 13 hours in the same test. The Erazer Defender 17 P10 is at least quick to charge, though, taking between an hour and 90 minutes to fully replenish. Should I buy the Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10? You won’t find many large gaming laptops with such a capable spec for less. Content is surprisingly vibrant with good levels of contrast, while the 1080p resolution is just sharp enough for the 17-inch size. In terms of looks and material quality, the Erazer Defender 17 P10 is unlikely to wow you. A 17-inch gaming laptop is never going to be easy to carry around, and although the Erazer Defender 17 P10 does well to keep its weight and dimensions down, it’s still a chore to lug around. Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 review: Also consider The Erazer Major 16 X1 is more expensive than the Erazer Defender 17 P10, but it’s still good value when you consider its spec is better in just about every way. This includes its display resolution, which is much sharper at 1600p, although it’s smaller at 16 inches. Read our full Medion Erazer Major 16 X1 review. The V16 is much cheaper than the Erazer Defender 17 P10, although its overall spec is weaker: most notably when it comes to its RTX 4050 GPU. However, it has the same 1080p resolution, and is surprisingly portable for a large gaming laptop. Read our full Asus V16 review. How I tested the Medion Erazer Defender 17 P10 I tested the Erazer Defender 17 P10 for a few days, gaming with it as well as using it for working and streaming video content. I ran our series of benchmark tests, designed to assess every facet of a gaming laptop’s performance. I also ran a movie on a continuous loop to test its battery life. I’ve been PC gaming for over a decade, and have used a variety of builds and components in that time. I’ve also reviewed numerous gaming laptops before, across all shapes, sizes, specs, and budgets.

item.title: REVIEW: The new Onyx Boox Note Air6 C is just the last-gen Note Air5 C masquerading as a new release
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Onyx Boox Note Air6 C is the latest Android-powered eReader from Onyx Boox. The brand always knocks it out of the park with its spunky E Ink tablets, offering native OCR, fantastic reading and writing apps, and unrestricted access to the Google Play Store in slim, trim metal bodies. Boox always keeps good on its software promise, delivering timely updates in the three-year timespan of guaranteed software support. The 10.3-inch Note Air6 C follows in the footsteps of the Note Air5 C, which came out a year ago. The brand also released a couple of smaller models alongside the Note Air6 C. Among all the releases, I find the Boox Picco to be the most unique pick of the lot, as it breaks the status quo and offers a unique experience. I'm afraid I can't say the same for the Note Air C series from Boox because the last three generations have been nearly identical. Going into this review, I was really hoping that Boox made noteworthy changes with the Note Air6 C. Enjoy the best of ePaper with the 10.3-inch Onyx Boox Note Air6 C. Powered by a 4nm octa-core processor, it runs Android 16 and gives you unbridled access to the Google Play Store. Reading and writing is a premium experience on this eye-friendly, stylus bearing tablet. - 64GB, expandable up to 2TB via microSD - PDF, CAJ, DJVU, CBR, CBZ, EPUB, EPUB3, AZW3, MOBI, TXT, DOC, DOCX, FB2, CHM, RTF, HTML, ZIP, PRC, PPT and PPTX, plus PNG, JPG, BMP, TIFF, WAV and MP3 - The best native apps and features of any E Ink tablet - Top-notch hardware with expandable storage - Features like BOOXDrop and BOOXDrop Screen Mirroring are unrivalled - Almost exactly the same as previous-gen iteration Onyx Boox launched the Onyx Boox Note Air6 C on September 16, 2026. The Note Air6 C is priced at $579.99 and comes with a Boox Pen3 stylus in the box. Accessories such as the magnetic folio case and the keyboard case are sold separately, with the basic case going for $50.99 and the keyboard case selling for $109.99. In contrast, the previous iteration is still up for grabs and costs $529.99 for almost the same specs, though the accessories cost the same. Did this even warrant a new release? The Onyx Boox Note Air6 C has the hallmarks of a great Android eReader. The sleek chassis is exceedingly thin, measuring just 5.8mm thick, and the body weighs a mere 440g. In comparison, the Samsung Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra weighs 692g and measures 5.1mm thick. The power button has a fingerprint sensor incorporated within it and is situated on top. The right side has volume buttons and is magnetic, so the Boox Pen3 stylus can be docked. Boox reinforced the magnetic strength of the stylus docking side, as the stylus used to fall off quite easily on the Note Air5 C. Apart from the slight difference in color, the two Note Air series tablets are virtually indiscernible from one another. I wish Boox had changed the stylus, because I hate the Boox Pen3 with a passion. The writing experience is lovely, and you get that scratchy feel when etching on the ePaper screen. My beef with the stylus is its poorly designed nib storage compartment on the back with a magnetic cap. The nibs always fall out, and at this point I have lost all my spare nibs from the previous Pen3. Older styli worked perfectly fine, but Boox decided to fix what wasn't broken. A perfectly good stylus has been replaced by an annoying one. The 10.3-inch E Ink Kaleido 3 display with front lights is the main attraction. The large, color screen is perfect for graphic novels and comics. Users can adjust brightness, color temperature, other color settings, and screen refresh modes on the fly. Boox paired this display with solid hardware specs like Bluetooth 6, Wi-Fi, stereo speakers, a mic, a 4nm Qualcomm 6690 processor, a BSR GPU, 6GB RAM, 64GB onboard memory, a microSD port that supports up to 2TB of expansion, a 3,700mAh battery, and a USB-C port with 15W wired charging. The Note Air6 C retains the magnetic pogo pins from the Note Air5 C that connect the Boox keyboard case wirelessly. Because of this, you can use the Note Air5 C keyboard case with the newer model. With light use, the battery lasts for weeks. With heavier use, you can still get several days of use out of a full charge. It charges at a snail's pace, supporting only 15W wired charging via USB-C. Ghosting is noticeably better than in past generations, and the tablet lets you force-refresh the screen at any time to clear lingering ink particles. Another fantastic feature is USB-C OTG support, which lets you connect a USB-C flash drive or supported device. The new 4nm octa-core processor is a smidge faster than the one from the last Note Air C tablet, but it's hardly noticeable unless you actively push the device to its limits. I genuinely don't think there are sufficient hardware changes to warrant a new release. I don't see why Onyx Boox didn't wait a little longer between releases. The E Ink Corp just unveiled E Ink Spectra 6 9-Color, the latest color E Ink display tech that features better vibrancy thanks to a nine-color base. We've been seeing the same hardware since the Note Air3 C was released in 2023. Three years on, Onyx Boox had the opportunity to give a huge display upgrade to the series, but decided to fumble hard instead. Boox sticks it in the face of Kindle and Kobo Any Onyx Boox tablet runs the same OS, so you get a consistent experience across models. The Boox Note Air6 C runs BOOX Firmware V4.3 based on Android 16 out of the box. You get all the base elements of Android, from the notification panel and status bar to gesture navigation and extensive settings. The Google Play Store lets you download any app you could want, from the Kindle Store and Audible to Google Chrome and Spotify. What sets Boox apart is its excellent suite of native apps and tools. I love the Boox Notes App for note-taking, rough sketching, and general writing. The native OCR converts handwritten text really well, and you can even write into any text input field on the entire tablet. Calendar Memo lets you take notes, write down memos, create reminders, and add events. You sync third-party calendars and apps with it too, such as Google Calendar, Microsoft To Do, and CaLDAV. The built-in reading app, NeoReader, syncs your progress online, offers an exhaustive set of options and settings, and supports a very wide range of file formats. The Note Air6 C supports PDF, CAJ, DJVU, CBR, CBZ, EPUB, EPUB3, AZW3, MOBI, TXT, DOC, DOCX, FB2, CHM, RTF, HTML, ZIP, PRC, PPT and PPTX, plus PNG, JPG, BMP, TIFF, WAV and MP3. There is no dedicated data-copying feature between old and new Boox tablets, like Samsung Smart Switch or Google's native Android-to-Android data-copying tool. But thanks to OTG support, I managed to connect my old Note Air5 C to the Note Air6 C and copied my eBooks and files over. Apps still have to be installed manually. There were also some minor glitches on the tablet, though they were noticeably fewer than what I faced on the Note Air5 C at launch. This is a given with any new smartphone or tablet, however. What's important is that Boox always addresses issues and releases firmware updates and patches quite frequently. I am anticipating an over-the-air update to iron them out. Should you buy the Onyx Boox Note Air6 C? You should buy the Onyx Boox Note Air6 C if: - You don't own an Android eReader already - You want at least three years of guaranteed software updates - You need a reliable E Ink tablet for reading and writing - You want the best software experience on an eReader You should not buy the Onyx Boox Note Air6 C if: My verdict regarding the Note Air6 C is two-fold and depends on the context. On the one hand, it is a sleek piece of hardware that performs well, is jam-packed with features, and has reliable software updates. It is a stunning, well-made tablet overall. But on the other hand, it does not add anything worth your attention over the last-gen Note Air5 C. Even though the processor has been upgraded, the difference in real-life performance between the two tablets is entirely negligible. If you are new to the world of Android eReaders, I say go for the latest and greatest, just so you're guaranteed to get software updates for another three years from now. There's a $50 price difference between the two, which is worth an extra year of OS updates. However, if you're thinking about upgrading your existing Onyx Boox Note Air5 C to the newest model, don't do it. Your old Boox is still supported for two more years. Wait for the brand to add significant changes to the Note Air C series; you'll actually get a proper upgrade. The key takeaway is that Onyx Boox makes excellent Android eReaders, but the brand needs to do a major refresh of the Note Air C lineup instead of re-releasing the same product for the fourth time. You can't go wrong with a Boox tablet, but choosing the newest model isn't necessary. It doesn't add much to the previous-gen Note Air 5C, but the Onyx Boox Note Air 6C is the latest Android eReader from the brand. Equipped with handy tools like a stylus and a stunning E Ink screen, this is easily one of the most premium eReaders out there.

item.title: REVIEW: Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 review: A quiet and compact Wildcat
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Minisforum’s smallest and cheapest mini PC packing Intel's Wildcat Lake silicon is here. It is small, quiet, and easy to stow away, but this machine's performance is really only for light workloads. - +Capable enough for home office and media consumption - -Only old or lightweight games and emulators are playable - -Not a cheap option unless you have spare parts and go barebones Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Minisforum’s Intel-based M2 line includes mini PCs with powerful processors such as the Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H (with 16C/16T CPU and B390 graphics), and the Core Ultra 7 356H (16C/16T). But there are more modest systems, too. The M2 Air-304 here is the most affordable option, based around the Intel Core 3 processor 304 with its 5C/5T CPU (1x Cougar Cove P-core and 4x Darkmont LP E-cores) and an iGPU with just a single Xe3 core. No surprise, the little brother in the pack, both in terms of physical size and computing resources, is the most affordable. It currently starts at $263 for a barebones version. However, our test sample with 16GB DDR5-5600, a 500GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro is listed at $559 - direct. That’s an introductory price, and Minisforum’s small text threatens that our configuration will bump up to $699 at some point in the future. Such a rise would put this product offering on very shaky ground, and we see B&H Photo has already raised the price at $729. Overall, this Mini PC was pleasant to use, though. It ran quietly and only strained in gaming and productivity benchmarks which put it under loads that casual users aren’t going to be running on such a machine. Design of the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 Mini PC The Mini M2 Air looks stylish enough, and feels solid. Looks can be deceiving, though, and the top shell is a silver colored plastic, not a metallic alloy. Sometimes a metal shell can be used to help conduct away heat, but that seems less important with this actively cooled machine with a 15W processor. We note that there are thermal pads connecting the installed RAM and SSD to the bottom of this mini PC, which is metal. A VESA mounting bracket is provided in the box if you prefer to hide the tiny device out of sight. It doesn’t have a remote power switch like the MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG we reviewed earlier in the year, though, so you’ll have to consider reachability. A simple LED-lit power button is on the front of the device, alongside a couple of handy ports (more on the ports later). It also has a reset / clear CMOS hole on the front, and a Kensington lock slot on the rear. Minisforum’s component choices mean this is a particularly small and light mini PC. The official M2 Mini specs state it is 112 x 112 x 37.15mm, which is roughly 4.4 x 4.4 x 1.5-inches. That’s a volume of 0.47 liters. It weighs in at just 440 grams, which is 0.97 pounds. The power supply isn’t built-in. There’s a surprisingly bulky 65W power brick in the box, which connects to using a detachable figure-eight cable. However, this mini PC can be powered by USB-C, too, so you could pack a far more compact multipurpose power brick if portability is important. Specifications of the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 Mini PC On the front of the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 there are 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 ports and a 3.5mm audio jack. Turn it to the side and you’ll see the microSD card slot. Then, around the back you have access to 1x USB4 (40Gbps, DP Alt Mode, PD), 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 1x USB 2.0, 2x HDMI 2.0, 2x RJ-45 2.5GbE LAN, and a DC-IN barrel jack. Some might like to have at least one of the Type-C ports on the front, instead of two Type-As. But for its size the Mini M2 Air packs quite a few ports, including the very capable USB4, two HDMI ports, and two Ethernet ports. Realistically, a machine like this won’t be connected to oodles of wired peripherals, but if you found the port count lacking, USB4 allows for a capable and fast dock. Wireless connectivity seems adequate, with an M.2 2230 card inside providing Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.4. I had no problems with either during the test period. The wireless card is socketed. It's located under the SSD, making it easy to repair or upgrade down the line. Accessing the components inside the Minisforum Mini M2 Air is straightforward, but you need to peel off all the four rubber feet to get to four long fastening screws. When they’re removed, just flip off the metal bottom to access the M.2 slots and SODIMM. Be aware there’s some adhesive force holding this metal plate in place, due to the sticky thermal pads on the RAM and storage. There’s just a single M.2 2280 storage slot and one SODIMM slot, both populated. That means, there’s no way to upgrade the RAM than swapping the module you already have in place. Our sample came with a 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM, but the system supports up to DDR5-6400. This only non-barebones configuration also came with a 500GB SSD in the M.2 slot. Productivity Performance on the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 We have Intel’s latest 18A silicon inside this tiny PC, but not that much of it. Our review unit came with an Intel Core 3 304 "Wildcat Lake" chip that runs up to 4.3 GHz. Previous mini PCs based on Intel 300 series mobile silicon like the previously MSI and the GMKtec Evo-T2 came with a 16C/16T CPU. However, here we have just 5C/5T, and that’s just one performance core supported by four low power efficiency (LPE) cores. Still, single core performance continues to be important for system and app responsiveness. The proof of the pudding is in the testing, though. And while this system felt perfectly usable in Windows 11, internet browsers, and word processing — preparing and writing this review, for example — the benchmarks are somewhat tougher. As we expected, the single core tests show Wildcat Lake has some bite. It easily beats its AMD-based rivals in the POV Ray single core rendering tests, for example. Moreover, in tests like Cinebench 2024 single core, the Mini M2 Air might trail the pack, but not by very much. It's roughly 107 points is actually within touching distance of the 120 points scored by ‘high performance’ mini PCs like the Beelink SER10 MAX (Gorgon Point) and MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG (Panther Lake). Multicore tests exposed obvious weaknesses of the 5C/5T CPU configuration with single-channel RAM. All the other mini PCs we’ve tested this year come with 12C/24T (AMD) or 16C/16T (Intel), so the productivity benchmarks we run which can take advantage of multithreading for demanding rendering or encoding tasks make the Minisforum here seem weak. However, it might still be acceptable for transcoding a short video or two, occasionally, as long as you aren’t in a rush. If you are coming from an older, less efficient desktop sporting something like an i7-7700K or i5-10400, this 15W Wildcat Lake chip is an improvement in both single and multicore performance. During our demanding tests, the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 stayed cool and quiet thanks to its 15W processor and capable cooling. Gaming and Graphics on the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 For anything other than the most casual gaming or emulation of older consoles you should look at other devices. We’ve looked at Intel 300 silicon powered devices with iGPUs packing 12 Xe3 cores, and four Xe3 cores, but this just has one, and it is further hampered by sharing the single-channel system RAM. Prepare to see some low frame rates / scores in our standard tests. I felt that some of these tests probably shouldn’t be run on this mini PC, but did it anyway, for completeness. However, some 3DMark benchmarks simply wouldn’t run, as Intel has pruned the features that work on this iGPU due to limited resources. For example, 3DMark Solar Bay doesn’t run on this system, and neither does Speed Way. Error messages about unsupported hardware pop up when you try these tests. Steel Nomad ran, though, and the Minisforum and its solo Xe3 core achieved a score of 135. The aforementioned Evo-T2 with Intel Core Ultra X7 358H and (B390) iGPU with 12x Xe3 cores scored 1,624. That’s incredibly close to 12x faster than the Core 3 304’s ‘Intel Graphics.’ A score of 135 means Steel Nomad ran at just a little more than 1 FPS, which actually doesn’t hurt your eyes to watch as much as 10 FPS. Using the multi-scene benchmarks built into Shadow of the Tomb Raider and Cyberpunk 2077 using our standard settings selections resulted in some unpleasant experiences. Performance of no better than 10 or 12 FPS was observed in these tests. To achieve 25 or even 30 FPS in these titles I found that reducing the game resolution to 720p and low/lowest settings would just about get there. So, for some actual fun on the Mini M2 Air I decided to try the latest version of the Sony PSP emulator PPSSPP and play some Wipeout Pure. I managed to run this game on my 1440p monitor with a 6x render resolution, and it achieved a nice steady 60 FPS, delivering an enjoyable futuristic racing experience. It would also therefore likely be good for retro emulation of similar era and older consoles as well as home computers. Power, Heat, and Noise when using the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 During my day-to-day use, the Minisforum system consumed around 9W when idling on the desktop. When under the heaviest loads I threw at it, the highest system power consumption I saw was around 31W. I didn't find it surprising that this low-power system ran cool and quiet. System tools showed that during light activities like browsing the web the CPU temperature remained in the low 30s Celsius. Playing games or benchmarking for length periods, I never saw the reported CPU temperature rise beyond the low 70s Celsius. Minisforum’s tiny mini PC was a quiet operator at idle and under load. My measurements from about half a foot in front of the device show noise levels under 30 dBA at idle, which is very quiet and actually said to be beneath the measurement threshold of my meter. Stressing the system with simultaneous CPU and GPU loads I managed to observe just a reading of a little over 37 dBA from the system. Software and Warranty on the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 The Mini M2 Air ships with Windows 11 Pro installed in the configuration we received. I found no pre-installed bloatware. The official specs don’t mention compatibility with other OSes like Linux. Minisforum sells this mini PC with a two-year warranty and a 30-day money-back guarantee. Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 configurations Minisforum sells only two Elite Mini M2 Air-304 configurations in the U.S. There’s a barebones model, or the configuration we tested with pre-installed RAM, SSD, and OS. At the time of writing our 16GB / 500GB / Windows 11 Pro configuration is listed by the mini PC maker at $559 but the product page says the price is normally $699. The barebone model is currently $263, discounted from $329. We don’t know when the prices might get adjusted. However, we’ve noted U.S. retailers like B&H Photo are now selling the 16GB / 500GB model at $729. Though the Mini M2 Air’s performance may lack in performance, it also probably the smallest cheapest, and least power-hungry mini PC we’ve tested all year. If these kinds of qualities are important to you, the Minisforum might be appealing. It is admirable that this mini PC is so small but leaves RAM and storage upgrades on the table for later. Other positives are the sturdy build, despite the use of plastic for the top shell, and a good port selection considering its size. In addition to being easy to hide due to its small stature, and supplied VESA mount, you probably won’t hear it very much, either. Of course, the performance is a weakness that can’t be ignored, especially in the context of our ever-growing tested mini PCs chart from 2026. It is great to see this latest-gen processor barebones at just over $260 direct from Minisforum. If you have a spare DDR5 SODIMM and SSD, perhaps from a laptop upgrade or wherever, this might help you get a new mini PC system up and running cheaply. However, the 16GB RAM and 500GB SSD (and Windows 11 Pro license) currently more than doubles the list price (it adds $296). That’s a bit painful. Furthermore, if the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air ever rises to its apparent MSRP of $699, we’d definitely look elsewhere. Around this price, especially during sale periods, you can shop for mini PCs employing far more powerful previous-gen processors. One good alternative candidate might be the Geekom IT13 Max 2026 we reviewed in August at $799. Price trackers show this Core Ultra 185H machine with 24GB RAM has been available for under $600 with discount / coupon over the last few months. There are also a lot of capable older gen AMD mini PCs to ponder over at attractive prices.

item.title: REVIEW: Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR review: just the ticket for sprawling lawns with heavy undulations
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Renowned robot vac manufacturer Roborock waltzes into the autonomous lawn mower arena with a seriously impressive wire-free model that combines rock-solid laser-guided navigation with some genuinely ingenious engineering. It’s called the RockMow Z120 LiDAR, and its clever front-wheel arrangement and suspension system give it the agility and stability to tackle uneven terrain with confident aplomb, while its generous 24cm floating cutting deck delivers an impressively consistent parallel finish. Add the optional side-mounted edge cutter and you have one very sophisticated and thoughtfully engineered machine that makes autonomous lawn care mostly effortless. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR: two-minute review For a first timer on the sward, the new Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR has proven to be an extremely impressive piece of lawn-care engineering, combining sophisticated LiDAR navigation with a host of clever mechanical flourishes that give its competitors a very good run for their monies. But then one shouldn’t be too surprised by this, given that the Chinese behemoth is already such a well-established leader in the field of autonomous indoor floor cleaners. The Z120’s rock-solid LiDAR and VSLAM navigation has worked wonders on my tree-lined lawn, while its ingenious front-wheel arrangement has enabled it to make tight turns without ripping the lawn to shreds. Add a proper suspension system, floating 24cm cutting deck and the ability to climb slopes of up to 80 degrees, and you have a wire-free mower that easily handles a myriad of lawn layouts. Having spent some time with the RockMow Z120, it's difficult not to be impressed by the sheer amount of thought that has gone into its design. As a result, its accurate LiDAR navigation, impressive obstacle avoidance, clever front wheels, neat cutting results and insane ability to scale the steepest of slopes make this model a must-have for those with large lawns – and those who can afford the premium price tag. Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR: price & availability - How much does it cost? £2,299 / €2,799 - When is it available? Available now, launched May 2026 in UK The Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR is firmly positioned in the premium end of the robotic lawn mower market, and its price reflects the considerable tranche of technology on board, particularly its clever articulating front wheels. In the UK, the Z120 LiDAR has an official retail price of £2,299 (about $3,030 / AU$4,500) with Roborock UK currently selling it for £2,069.10. However, I've also spotted it advertised for considerably less at Donaghy Bros where it’s selling for a knockdown £1,599. Across Europe, the Z120 is called the Z1 and is generally marketed at around €2,799 — a whopping price to pay, and that’s without the optional PreciEdge side-cutting module which costs around €150. In the USA, the equivalent model is sold as the RockMow X1 LiDAR, with a recommended retail price of $3,199. For a robotic mower, these are serious sums of money, but the Z120's sophisticated LiDAR navigation, four-wheel drive train, clever front wheel system and impressive cutting performance go some way towards justifying the investment. Nevertheless, there are other all-terrain models out there that compete very favourably with the RockMow Z120 LiDAR, most notably the four-wheel-drive, LiDAR and RTK-equipped Mammotion LUBA 3 (£2,049), which has a much wider cutting deck but not as good a front-wheel drive system. Also check out the Segway Navimow i210E LiDAR Pro which comes with three-wheel drive, Xero-Turn and a cutting range of up to 1,000m². - Unique front wheel system reduces tearing Given Roborock’s leadership in the field of floor cleaning robotics — specifically in the navigation and obstacle avoidance departments — I can think of no better corporation to join the current throng of robot lawnmower manufacturers. In fact, in April 2025 I fired off an email to my contact at Roborock to enquire — off the record — whether the company would ever consider producing a robotic lawn mower. His answer? "I can't share anything about that... yet!" Well, lo and behold, here they come — and the prognosis is good. Very good. For the record, in the UK where this review is being written, Roborock’s opening salvo of Euro-spec robot mowers is comprised of six core model variants across three product platforms — the RockNeo Q series, RockMow S series and RockMow Z series — with expanded options like the flagship LiDAR-equipped Z120 I’m reviewing here. Despite being a highly-regarded robot vacuum cleaner manufacturer with a great reliability record, the company is facing stiff opposition from several established manufacturers like Segway, Mammotion, TerraMow, Worx, Anthbot and Husqvarna. On the other hand, garden robotics is still a relatively new industry, and it’s not like no one’s ever heard of Roborock. In fact, it’s quite likely that the company’s first swathe of interested parties will come from its own highly established user base. After all, if you’re happy with a brand, love its products and the app that runs them, why not stick with what you know? The new Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR’s angular wedge-shaped body, prominent rear suspension springs, and chunky, deeply treaded wheels both fore and aft give it a rugged, almost miniature off-road vehicle appearance that I find very appealing. In fact, just lifting its substantial 21.7kgs (47.84lbs) of weight should reassure any new owners of rough, complex landscapes that they made the right decision. While the Z120 doesn’t sport the wider cutting tract of Mammotion’s hardy LUBA series, I can see this model becoming an incredibly popular alternative, partly because of its four-wheel drive ability to scale steep inclines of up to 80%, but mostly because its front wheels independently articulate to near 90 degrees, enabling to make tight turns without churning up shady areas of the lawn. Let’s look at this model in more detail. Roborock has addressed some of the complaints aimed at Mammotion’s LUBA range of mowers, which have fixed front wheels fitted with smaller omnidirectional spinners that allow the robot to make tight turns. The trouble with this system is that the spinners can quite easily loosen the earth around weaker grass stems as the robot turns on its axis, especially in shaded areas of the lawn. While I’ve never experienced any lawn scuffing, there are many LUBA users out there who have. By contrast, the RockMow Z120's drive system combines four-wheel drive with independent wheel motors and a very clever active steering system that allows both front wheels to swivel independently through almost 90 degrees in either direction when turning. Hence, the Z120 can execute zero-turn maneuvers without dragging its tires across the grass and ripping out the roots. This is a particularly useful feature when navigating shaded tree areas, flowerbeds and obstacles like trampolines, while also minimizing turf damage on slopes. The Z120’s four-wheel-drive system provides traction across all four corners, while the substantial rear wheels and independent suspension help maintain contact with even the most gnarly of ground. Believe me, this system works. Furthermore, Roborock claims the Z120 can tackle gradients of up to 80%, equivalent to around 39 degrees, and negotiate obstacles up to 8cm high, which is something the vast majority of mowbots are incapable of. This unusually sophisticated drive arrangement shows that Roborock’s R&D department clearly followed the working methods of practically every other wireless robot mower on the market and found ways of circumventing most of the issues that have plagued some of its competitors. By watching and learning — and holding back until it had perfected a drive system capable of meeting a wide variety of terrains — the Chinese robot vac manufacturer has burst out of the gates with a model that is near perfect when it comes to negotiating rough, wildly undulating terrain without destroying the very thing it was designed to maintain. The RockMow Z120 LiDAR uses a 21.6V, 6Ah lithium-ion battery that provides up to 110 minutes of mowing on a single charge. Like all robot mowers, when the battery’s depleted it automatically returns to its charging station, with a recharge taking approximately 50 minutes. Roborock claims a daily lawn coverage of up to 2,000m² for this model — a substantial half acre — so it’s clearly aimed at the higher end of lawn ownership. The Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR uses a single, centrally mounted 24cm cutting disc rather than the much wider twin-deck 40cm arrangement found on its closest rival, the Mammotion LUBA 3. Mind, 24cm of cutting width isn’t too bad for a single cutting disc model given that the norm is nearer 20cm. No, it won't create the appealingly wide cutting stripes of the LUBA 3 but the results are definitely better looking than the average 20cm model. The Z120’s cutting system carries six spinning blades that are partly hidden behind an aluminum disc to help cut down on grass wrapping around the blades’ connecting screws and eventually causing the blades to jam — a common occurrence with other robot mowers. While six blades might not sound particularly generous for a machine aimed at larger lawns, you have to remember that robotic mowers are designed to deliver a consistent finish through regular, automated mowing two or three times a week, so having three more blades than the average bot can be considered a bonus. Like all good lawnbots, the ZI20 is fitted with an electrically adjustable cutting height system that is accessed via the Roborock app. The cutting height ranges from 20mm to 70mm in 5mm increments, which covers practically every type of grass on the planet. And because the cutting deck is of the floating kind, it follows changes in ground level to maintain an even cut across uneven terrain. One particularly useful feature with this machine is the optional PreciEdge side-mounted cutting module. This adds a separate, smaller cutting disc with two blades, allowing the mower to trim much closer to boundaries, walls and fences than the main cutting deck can manage. The PreciEdge module is said to reach within 3cm to 5cm of an edge, although the actual result would depend on the boundary itself and if there are any overhanging plants. The PreciEdge side cutter is sold separately, mind, so you'll need to factor another £150 into the price if neat lawn edges are a priority. Just be aware that the PreciEdge has a fixed cutting height of 40mm so if you’re in the UK and prefer a 30mm cut, you can expect the edges to be 10mm longer. Since my preferred sweet spot in the UK is 35mm, I’m not too fussed by the negligible 5mm difference in height between the main part of the lawn and the edges. Roborock is a past master when it comes to robot vacuum cleaner navigation so I expected rock-solid reliability with this model. I was right, because this mower has behaved superbly well on my modest 170m² lawn. The RockMow Z120 LiDAR's navigation system uses Roborock's ‘Sentisphere Environmental Perception’ technology, which combines a 360-degree 3D LiDAR scanner with autonomous vehicle-style VSLAM (Visual Simultaneous Location and Mapping) and two cameras to build a detailed picture of its surroundings and determine its position, day or night. Unlike conventional robot mowers that depend on satellite positioning using, in many cases, an RTK antennae spiked into the ground, this LiDAR version requires no such malarky. Instead, its rotating laser sensor continuously scans the garden, measuring distances to surrounding objects and using these measurements to establish its position, in much the same way as robot vacuum cleaners get about the house. This makes the Z120 particularly well suited to gardens with dense tree cover, shaded areas and complicated layouts where satellite signals are often unreliable. Crucially, the Z120’s navigation system also supports systematic mowing rather than the random wandering associated with older robot mowers. Once the lawn has been mapped, the Z120 starts a parallel cutting route in any direction the user wants. This method ensures that the Z120 covers the entire lawn efficiently while leaving a consistent Wimbledon-like striped finish in its wake. In fact, I wager that it’s the pretty lawn stripes that has ultimately made the modern robotic lawn mower so incredibly popular. That and the huge amount of time it saves. While I’m not sure how many different garden zones this model can handle, I have heard that it’s around 15 and that’s about par for the course. As with other models, you simply map two or three different lawns and join them all together virtually in the Roborock app by manually steering the Z120 from one lawn to the next. As long as there are no obstacles like stairs and gates en route, the Z120 will cut one lawn before following the path to the next zone, and so on and so forth. The RockMow Z120 LiDAR employs an impressive obstacle avoidance system that’s designed to identify and negotiate the various hazards that inevitably litter a real-world garden, like toys, stray plant pots, hose sprinklers, etc. Using a combination of LiDAR and onboard VSLAM technology, it can detect most objects in its path and adjust its trajectory accordingly. A collision sensitive bumper adds extra peace of mind. The Roborock app offers two main levels of adjustable obstacle avoidance sensitivity – Mowing Coverage Priority and Obstacle Avoidance Priority. If you have kids who may be on the lawn, you can also set Proximity Pause so the mower either avoids them or stops working altogether. And, like quite a few other models, this one also has a Wildlife-Friendly mode that stops operation during specified hours, which is usually during the night. The Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR has a pretty comprehensive anti-theft package, which is reassuring given that this is an extremely expensive piece of garden kit that’s usually left unattended outdoors. That said, all modern robot mowers are indelibly linked to the owner’s account and Wi-Fi system so even if a thief were to steal it, it would basically be a brick. The trouble is that most thieves won’t know this so it’s still always a good thing to activate any security options in the app. For the record, the Z120’s security features include a PIN code lock, a high-decibel alarm, and built-in 4G connectivity for real-time location tracking through the Roborock app. The alarm can be configured to activate if the mower is lifted or moved beyond its preset virtual boundary, though I should add that I haven’t been able to lower the app’s default minimum of 100m on my test unit, which is way too far beyond its working perimeter for my liking. Perhaps a future update will allow for a shorter distance of, say, 25m If the Z120 does go walkabout, you can check its location through the app and remotely activate the alarm to attract attention. Since the 4G tracking facility requires the mower to be switched on, Roborock has also provided a hidden compartment beneath the top shell for an additional third-party tracking device like an Apple AirTag, which provides another potential way of recovering it if stolen. Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR: performance I apologize on behalf of the British weather this summer because, while a very long spell of hot dry weather in the UK is always welcome for most of us, this year’s series of heatwave followed by drought conditions turned the English landscape into the African bush veldt, making it nigh-on impossible for reviewers to accurately appraise most garden products. Thankfully rain did eventually arrive and the grass recovered to some degree so I could properly test this mower. Here are some of its most valid performance stats. The RockMow Z120 LiDAR is a hefty brute of a mower, so you may need two to get it out of the box and carry it to where you plan to site the charging station — Roborock provides about 10m of cable to your nearest outdoor AC outlet. Set up is extremely easy because it doesn’t involve staking in any ancillary RTK antennae. Instead, you simply position the charging base as advised in the manual, plug it in and roll the Z20 onto the charging pins. Now launch the Roborock app, tap + and follow the onscreen instructions for an extremely fuss-free set up. Once activated, the first thing you’ll need to do is map your lawn for the first time, and you can do this in two ways — automatically or manually, by steering the Z120 around the perimeter of your lawn. Like all auto-mapping bots, the the Z120 will head out of its dock and proceed to hug the entire border of a lawn using both its LiDAR laser system and the two front-mounted cameras. Auto mapping is a good choice if your lawn has a simple layout and the borders don’t have any plants overhanging. Like most reviewers, I personally prefer using the manual method since I can steer it more accurately along the border and under any overhanging foliage. This method should ensure that all future cuts are as close to the edge as possible. However, I should point out that the default steering mechanism uses just one multidirectional virtual joystick on the app instead of the normal two — one to move the robot forward and the other to make turns. I would suggest changing the single joystick to twin sticks in the app or you’ll be steering the robot all over the place and make a right hash of your first map. Now your lawn is mapped, you can set the Z120 off on its first run. Just don’t forget to change the cutting height in the app to a higher setting if your grass is on the long side or it will leave a trail of ugly clippings behind. Once your first cut is complete, you can lower the cutting height to somewhere in the region of 35mm — the sweet spot for UK lawns. When it comes to performance and day-to-day usability, the Roborock Z120 LiDAR has proven to be a remarkably accomplished piece of lawn-tending kit. Its navigation has been excellent on my admittedly simple lawn layout, with the mower confidently finding its way around the garden, negotiating boundaries and maintaining impressively straight, parallel cutting lines. The latter is particularly satisfying because, aside from ensuring consistent coverage, the neat, regimented passes have left some rather fetching lawn stripe in its wakes, and with no sign of any damage to my soft-soiled lawn when it's turning. Obstacle avoidance is another major strength. In my test, the Z120 demonstrated an impressive ability to recognize and negotiate around a long sausage-like dog toy, a very small cast-iron duck ornament, and a small flower pot that that flummoxed at least two models I’ve previously reviewed. It has also gone about its business without requiring any supervision or intervention, which is precisely what you want from a machine that's designed to take the hassle out of lawn mowing. I also tried the optional side-mounted edge cutter, which allows the Z120 to get considerably closer to lawn boundaries than most of the competition. It's a worthwhile, albeit pricy, addition though I will admit that it never quite managed to achieve a cut right to the very last few centimeters along the edge. In other words, don't throw away the grass trimmer just yet because you may still need it for the occasional bit of edge smartening. I’ll sign off with a massive shout-out to the Z120’s genuinely astonishing four-wheel-drive ability to climb steep slopes. I tested it on an extremely challenging gradient consisting of damp early-winter earth covered in wet leaves — hardly ideal conditions for maintaining traction — and was amazed at how confidently it scaled the bank on four separate occasions. As the accompanying video illustrates, the Z120 simply drove straight up the incline as though it were negotiating a level playing field. There was no hesitation, wheel spin or retreat back down the slope. It just flew up. For context, the Mammotion LUBA 3 also managed this same impressive feat, although my test of that mower was conducted on dry summer earth without the added complication of slippery, wet leaves. Top marks for this. Granted, this is an extraordinarily expensive model for most prospective robot mower buyers and way too sophisticated for conventional lawnscapes. But if you have a large complex garden with surrounding trees and several steep gradients that’s in excess of 1,500m² (about a third of an acre) and the readies to match, I would wholeheartedly recommend this beast, mostly because it does the job and does it so well. Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR: Roborock app If you’re already a Roborock robot vacuum owner, you’ll already be familiar with the app that controls the Z120. That's a definite bonus in my book even though the interface is polished, intuitive, and refreshingly easy for a first timer to grasp. From mapping your lawn and establishing mowing zones to setting schedules, adjusting cutting preferences, creating no-go areas, and setting your own security measures, pretty much everything is accessible from your smartphone without the need for a degree in IT. However, there are some areas for improvement, especially when it comes to the Z120’s mowing speed. At the moment its operational speed appears to be fixed to a medium-paced speed. I would like to see an option to change this to either slower or faster. Also, coming from the UK, I’d prefer to hear the robot’s voice notifications in an English-accented voice, as Roborock provides for its robot vac lineup. Should you buy the Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR? Your lawn is large and/or steeply undulating This model is a great choice for complex lawns and brilliant at scaling steep slopes The Z120 LiDAR’s articulating front wheels ensure that tight turns don’t mess up the lawn The Z120’s impressive obstacle avoidance vastly minimizes unwanted collisions This mower is overkill on smaller urban and suburban lawns The optional side cutter will help reduce the need for edge trimming, but it's not entirely successful Premium pricing puts this model way beyond many budgets How I tested the Roborock RockMow Z120 LiDAR I had a very late start testing this model because it arrived in July, just as the UK drought of 2026 took hold and the grass almost immediately went dormant. Nevertheless, the rains eventually returned so I could finally get it on the lawn to put it through its paces. As usual, I tested its mapping accuracy, noting how well it navigated my lawn, how well its six-blade cutting system performed, how efficiently it turned without ripping up edges of the lawn and how well it avoided obstacles. I’m pleased to say that, in most instances, it performed as well as the best models I’ve previously reviewed.

item.title: REVIEW: SteelSeries Aeon Pro review: this Xbox controller offers unlimited power — for a seriously premium price
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The SteelSeries Aeon Pro has so many game-changing features it’s hard to squeeze them all in. Both its dual-system connectivity and hot-swappable batteries make it so much more flexible than rival controllers, while its OLED screen, dual-mode triggers, and Hall effect thumbsticks all make it feel really versatile. Its control app makes switching profiles a breeze, although there are a few customization options missing. There’s no getting around that price, though: this is an expensive controller, even compared to its closest rivals. - -Can’t map system actions to rear paddles Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The SteelSeries Aeon Pro is a pro-level wireless controller compatible with PC and Xbox Series X / S. Not only does it offer many of the premium features you’d expect from a pad at its price point, but it also offers several huge innovations that separate it from other options in its class. Let’s start with the most attention-grabbing features. First off, the Aeon Pro offers dual-platform connectivity. That doesn’t mean it has a dongle you can swap between devices or use Bluetooth for your second system — its dock has dual outputs, meaning that you can flip its 2.4GHz Wi-Fi connectivity between PC and Xbox using the pad’s built-in OLED screen. As someone who regularly games on both, I loved how easy this made it to switch between them on the fly. But honestly, I’d say my favorite feature is SteelSeries’ Infinite Power System. Let’s set aside that slightly grandiose name: essentially, this means the Aeon Pro not only charges on its dock when not in use, but it also comes with hot-swappable rechargeable batteries. Every time I ran out of juice — which didn’t happen often, thanks to the pad’s 12-hour battery life — I could just swap in a fresh battery without having to resort to a cable, giving the Aeon Pro the edge over many of the best PC controllers. Elsewhere, the Aeon Pro’s design is similarly high-tier. Front and center, it features a built-in OLED screen, which allows you to switch between platforms and profiles straight from your controller. It also felt suitably ergonomic in my hands — every button sat right under my fingertips, even the rear paddles, while the textured grips made it easy to hang onto even during frantic pitched battles in FPS games. In use, the Aeon Pro is super responsive, thanks to its 1,000Hz polling rate. It also rocks dual-mode triggers, meaning you can switch between analog and micro-switch modes at the flip of a toggle. Meanwhile, both the triggers and thumbsticks are Hall effect — as a result, they’re rapid and drift-free, although they don’t offer quite the same sensitivity and energy efficiency as TMR alternatives. SteelSeries’ GG software also allows you to create potentially infinite custom profiles for different games, while you can load up to eight at a time onto the controller itself. On PC, you can also create profiles for each game in your library that then auto-switch when you fire the game up — I love the fact that I could have my thumbsticks automatically invert for games like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, particularly as these profiles are also compatible with SteelSeries’ Arctis Nova Pro Omni gaming headset as well. There are a couple of improvements I’d like to see to the SteelSeries GG app, though. First of all, unlike the software offered by rivals like Razer or ROG, GG doesn’t currently allow you any control over trigger response curves, and the options for the thumbsticks are pretty limited. Additionally, remapping only allows you to assign existing buttons from the controller to its back paddles — so if you were hoping to be able to tweak system controls or assign keyboard shortcuts there on PC, you’re out of luck. Aside from these niggles though, the only real hurdle for me is that price. Retailing at $259.99 / £229.99 / AU$529, it’s a pricey package, even compared to the best Xbox controllers, so it might not be the best fit for you if you’re looking for a bargain. But I’d argue that, with its swappable battery system and dual-platform connectivity, it gives a lot in return. So if you can afford it, you’re unlikely to come away disappointed with the SteelSeries Aeon Pro. SteelSeries Aeon Pro review: price and availability - List price of $259.99 / £229.99 / AU$529 - Comes with a lot of extras for your spend Having launched on September 8, 2026, the SteelSeries Aeon Pro is available now. Retailing at a list price of $259.99 / £229.99 / AU$529, it sits firmly at the premium end of the market. By way of comparison, the similarly pro Asus ROG Raikiri II Xbox Wireless has a list price of $189.99 / £199 / AU$349, while the Razer Wolverine V3 Pro originally retailed for $199.99 / £199.99 (around AU$290). So it’s not cheap, even compared to other pro controllers. But it is worth bearing in mind that the Aeon Pro comes with a dual-platform dock, two spare hot-swappable thumbsticks and two hot-swappable batteries, so you do get quite a lot for your cash. When it comes to your purchase options, SteelSeries’ controller comes in two colorways: black and the white version tested here. When you’re first setting up the SteelSeries Aeon Pro, you’ll likely notice that its dock has two USB-C outputs. That’s because the Aeon Pro is the first controller of its kind to offer dual-platform wireless connectivity. When I plugged it in to both my PC and Xbox Series X, I was able to switch between 2.4GHz connectivity to either system straight from the pad itself — this feels so much more fluid and intuitive than having to faff around with moving dongles or switch to Bluetooth pairing to use a different device. But for me, this isn’t the Aeon Pro’s most transformative feature. For that, we have to look under the hood: the SteelSeries’ Infinite Power System. Okay, don’t get carried away with visions of free-energy conspiracy theories — the Aeon Pro’s battery is definitely finite. But — as is the case with the recent SteelSeries Sensei and Rival Pro mice, as well as the Arctis Nova Pro Omni — it is replaceable and can be hot-swapped out for a full one, with the empty battery clipping into a charging port on the controller’s base. As a result, you should always have a full battery waiting in the wings to take over even when your current one is tapped, which is a really smart system. And the batteries are interchangeable with the Arctis Nova Pro Omni, meaning if you’re using both, you’ll always have a steady cycle of juiced-up power packs waiting in the wings. When you’ve popped in a charged battery and powered on the controller, the thing that will most grab your attention is that OLED smart display. While this is hardly the first pro controller we’ve seen with a screen, I would say this is one of the few I’ve seen that actually has a decent range of use cases. Not only does it allow you to flip between different game profiles, but you can also use it to switch sources between Xbox, PC, and Bluetooth, check battery levels, and even remap buttons on the fly. This definitely elevates it from gimmick to something I actually interacted with a lot. Elsewhere, the design looks smart and suitably pro, and the Aeon Pro feels nicely ergonomic. The gentle slant of its grips sat nicely in my hands, while their finely textured surface gave me a good amount of traction without getting too sweaty — something I can’t say of other controllers I’ve tested. Elsewhere, its body is fashioned from pleasantly tactile matte plastic and its build quality all feels appropriately premium, while still managing to weigh a light and floaty 10.9oz / 310g. For the most part, the Aeon Pro adopts the standard Xbox controller format, with asymmetrical thumbsticks. However, as a result of that OLED screen at the top of the pad, the start and menu buttons have been relocated to the bottom. I’ll admit this might be making virtue out of necessity, but this placement does actually feel preferable to me — rather than having to adjust your grip to reach past the left thumbstick or face buttons, you can just move your thumbs laterally and easily access in-game menus without stretching. Speaking of the thumbsticks, the Aeon Pro has moved away from drift-prone potentiometer-based sensors for its sticks, like most of its contemporaries. Personally, I’d prefer TMR-based thumbsticks and triggers for their marginally higher sensitivity, but the Hall-effect system used here is going to be plenty sufficient for all but professional esports players. And while TMR does provide a slight buff to energy efficiency, the Aeon Pro’s battery system should make this a bit of a non-issue. SteelSeries has offered another neat trick for this controller’s thumbsticks as well. Included with the Aeon Pro are two alternate sticks — these are magnetic and hot-swappable, meaning that I could quickly pop them off and replace them mid-game in a matter of moments. Another neat design decision here is the fact that the controller’s base has two magnetic docks for the sticks you aren’t using, which is just a thoughtful detail. I’ve raved before about how much I love dual-mode triggers, so I’m definitely pleased to see them included here on the Aeon Pro. Enabling you to switch between full-range analog and micro-switch triggers at the flip of a toggle, these give a controller huge versatility, whether you want sensitive control of an accelerator pedal in Forza Horizon 6 or want clicky, near-instant parries in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. All the Aeon Pro’s other buttons are similarly satisfying. Its face buttons also use micro-switches, feeling super accurate while giving immediate feedback. And its mappable rear paddles are perfectly positioned to sit under your fingertips, while feeling nice and snappy when you activate them. Everything feels easy to reach and quick to activate, which was fantastic when I needed to leap out of harm’s way or pull out my chainsaw to grind through imps in Doom. SteelSeries Aeon Pro review: performance All the innovative features in the world don't matter if a controller can't match them with powerful performance. Fortunately, the SteelSeries Aeon Pro doesn't struggle here in the least, offering snappy and fluid control over your games. Thanks to its 1,000Hz polling rate, the Aeon Pro has the reaction times of a hummingbird that’s just had its third energy drink of the day. Whether I was popping off headshots in FPSes or requiring precise steering to avoid flying off a hairpin bend in racing games, its thumbsticks always felt super responsive, and its micro-switch face buttons never betrayed a hint of lag. Dual-mode triggers are, once again, a totally worthwhile investment. When toggled on to their micro-switches, they aced my go-to test: helping me perform snappy parries and counters in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. With their assistance, I comfortably shrugged off even the remorseless combos of Aberrations. In their analog mode, the triggers feel fast and responsive — almost too fast, in fact, as occasionally while racing in Forza Horizon 6 I found myself wishing for a tiny bit more resistance to give me more granular control over my accelerator pedal. On the whole, SteelSeries GG software offers some fantastic features, although I did find it was lacking in a few options I’d come to take for granted from other brands’ apps. Not only does SteelSeries GG allow you to create, in theory, an infinite number of profiles, but you can load up to eight at a time on the Aeon Pro and flip between them using its OLED screen. That gives it far more flexibility than something like the Asus ROG Raikiri II, which requires you to swap back to its PC-only software just to change profiles. But even more innovative is its automatic profiles for your favorite PC games. For example, I was able to set my sticks to be directional rather than circular for the 2D platformer Hollow Knight: Silksong — then when I fired up the game, it automatically switched to the matching profile. Even better, this functionality also extends to the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni gaming headset, meaning I could set it to invert my thumbsticks and crank up the headset’s spatial audio every time I launched Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 without pressing a button. That honestly feels a little like magic. There’s a decent range of settings you can tweak in SteelSeries GG. These include remapping buttons and the back paddles, setting deadzones for the triggers and thumbsticks, adjusting the response of, or inverting, the sticks, altering the vibration of the grips and triggers, and tweaking the settings of that OLED screen. However, there are a few options I found myself missing here. First off, while you can change the response of the thumbsticks, there are only three options — default, dynamic, and exponential — while you can’t change the response of the triggers at all. That's a real shame, as I find the fully customizable curves that some apps offer are what really unlock the value of these tailor-made profiles; I definitely found myself missing S-shaped curves for controlling my pedal in Forza Horizon 6, for example. Secondly, while you can remap the rear paddles, you only seem to be able to set them up as shortcuts for existing buttons. There’s seemingly no way to set them to macros, control system-level functionality, or map them to in-game functions. I’d love to be able to use them to control my media player or bring up the quest menu in Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered, but the range of options is limited enough that it slightly hampers the paddles’ utility for me. Fortunately, these quibbles aren’t so severe that they detract from the Aeon Pro’s biggest draw for me: that battery system. It really can’t be overstated how fantastic it feels to never need to plug your pad in to charge. Not only did the full charge it got from its dock give me comfortably 12 hours of play per battery, but knowing I always had a full battery waiting in the wings meant I never had to experience range anxiety when I settled in for a marathon gaming sesh. Knowing I could play all weekend without ever needing to resort to an umbilical USB cable is a really freeing experience, and I’m here for it. Should I buy the SteelSeries Aeon Pro? Buy it if... Thanks to the Aeon Pro’s dual-platform system, you can switch between playing on your console and PC with the tap of a button — and without having to sacrifice 2.4GHz connectivity for either. You never want to run out of battery again Not only does the Aeon Pro charge when it’s on its base, but so does a backup hot-swappable battery, meaning you’ll never get caught short without charge during an epic GTA 6 session. Don't buy it if... Look, this almost goes without saying. But at $259.99 / £229.99 / AU$529, the Aeon Pro is an unabashedly premium controller. So if you’re looking for bargain prices, look elsewhere. While it’s crammed with great features like auto-detecting game profiles on PC, SteelSeries GG software has a few limitations like a lack of trigger response curves and an ability to map system functions to rear paddles. SteelSeries Aeon Pro review: also consider This is the Xbox and PC controller I use at home, and it’s fantastic. Not only does it have the 1,000Hz polling and dual-mode triggers that the Aeon Pro does, but it also rocks TMR thumbsticks and triggers and offers super customizable response curves in its control software. But it lacks SteelSeries’ awesome battery system and dual-platform connectivity, so it’s not an easy choice. Read my full Asus ROG Raikiri II Xbox Wireless review. There’s a reason that the Wolverine V3 Pro has sat as our best premium PC controller ever since its release. It offers fantastic performance, Hall effect sticks and triggers, dual-mode triggers, 1000Hz polling, and a wonderfully tactile playing experience. And while the fact that it’s slightly older means it lacks some of the latest features that the SteelSeries and Asus controllers do, it also means it comes in at a lower price, costing just $169.99 / £129.99 / AU$235.36. Read our full Razer Wolverine V3 Pro review. - Tried it with multiple devices and many types of games - Tweaked all of the available settings and created many custom profiles I tested the SteelSeries Aeon Pro over the course of a couple of weeks. I tested it extensively on both my Xbox Series X and on my desktop PC. On top of that, I made sure to test it on a wide variety of games, whether that was on adventure games like Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, racing games like Forza Horizon 6, RPGs like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, or FPSes like Doom. Endeavoring to test all of the Aeon Pro’s features, I tried out both its dual-source connectivity and swappable battery system. In addition, I tested all of the settings in SteelSeries’ control app, whether that was tweaking trigger and thumbstick settings, remapping buttons, or creating automatic gaming profiles. I also tested it alongside the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni to see how you can use profiles to switch up the settings of both simultaneously. When it comes to my own personal experience, I’ve been testing and writing about gadgets for over ten years. During that time, I’ve reviewed a range of controllers, headsets, and portable consoles. On top of that, I’ve been gaming for at least 35 years — having cut my teeth on early NES games, I’m now most likely to be gaming on my PC, Xbox Series X, Steam Deck, or Nintendo Switch 2.
