item.title: REVIEW: Tested: Alienware’s glorious 5K2K OLED monitor makes going big irresistible
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- The 330Hz, 1080p mode is too fuzzy at this size - Won’t fit well into a multi-monitor setup - Quickly shows OLED “shadows” The Alienware AW3926QW is a massive single OLED screen that can really show off the power of your gaming PC, without being too large to manage on a regular desk. It’s also gorgeous with its 5K2K panel, and offers plenty of flexible extras (like USB-C video with 90 watts) to justify its high price. It’s not the biggest or the cheapest out there, and I was underwhelmed by its speedy alt mode. But if you want incredible visuals with a centerpiece display, you won’t be disappointed. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Prices Today: Alienware AW3926QW 39-inch OLED 5K2K monitor The Alienware AW3926QW is an interesting middle ground for premium OLED gaming monitors. It’s big enough to give you some extra room to show off, and really push your hardware. But it’s not so massive that it becomes impractical for use at a regular desktop. Add in some nice extras, like USB-C video and dual-speed modes for the competitive gamers, and it’s an easy recommendation even at its premium price. Unboxing the Alienware AW3926QW, which I’m just going to call the “Alienware 39” from here on out, I was struck by how a few inches can make a big difference. (Stop that giggling.) You wouldn’t think that the jump from a 34-inch ultrawide, which I’ve been using on my own setup for years, to 39 inches at the same 21:9 aspect ratio, would be make such an impression. But it does. Sitting at a standard desk, it fills up my field of view almost edge to edge. And that’s before you take the resolution into account. The resolution, let’s talk about that for a moment. This is a 5K2K screen, 5120×2160. That, too, is an unexpectedly big jump over the 3440×1440 I’m used to. For me, a terminally addicted triple-monitor user, it was mostly more vertical space than I could really use, without the horizontal spacing that makes my working environment good for multi-tasking. You can read more about that hyper-specific experience here — suffice it to say that if you’re used to a multi-monitor setup, this might not have enough total space to satisfy you. But I don’t think this screen is intended to replace a multi-screen, productivity-focused setup, even if its price tag could buy three budget gaming screens. No, this is meant to be the visual component to a high-end setup, a companion to a powerful gaming PC that can make the most of its resolution and refresh rate. And I just so happen to have one. The Alienware is a fantastic way to show off your gaming desktop’s power. The huge panel just about fills my field of view sitting in a regular office chair, and its 5K2K resolution makes games like Star Wars: Galactic Racer really sing. You can see those details a lot better than on, say, the Samsung Odyssey G80HF with a similar total res but a screen about half the size. At its sharpest 5120×2160, the panel can handle “just” 165Hz, which is more than enough for me even in online competitive games. If you lower the resolution to 2560×1080, it boosts the maximum speed up to 330Hz. I’m guessing this will be a bit of a Sophie’s Choice for PC gamers who need the speed, as at a slightly wider 1080p and 39 inches, those virtual pixels at essentially four times the size start to be very noticeable. Comparing both modes in multiplayer bouts of Overwatch, I wasn’t able to see any real benefit to the 330Hz speed. It was barely smoother to my eyes, but as I have so recently said, I am old and my eyes aren’t great. If you’re a super-competitive gamer, you might get more mileage out of it. But if your eyes are better than mine, you’ll absolutely notice the “screen door effect,” as this mode effectively quadruples the size of each pixel. On the Alienware AW3926QW, it’s far more noticeable than on the Samsung with a similar half-res, double-speed dual mode. I get the feeling that most people will be running this thing at its full-power 5K2K splendor, even if they have to make sacrifices to hit 165Hz. On my RTX 5070 Ti machine, and even on the relatively forgiving Overwatch, I had to bump a few sliders to the left to hit that. What about other gaming and media capabilities? Well, you get support for VESA True Black 500, adaptive sync, Nvidia G-Sync, and eARC to work with sound bars. Diving into the OSD lets you enable an “esports mode” that restricts the size to 25 or 27 inches with a huge black margin, various crosshairs, a smart HDR toggle, and color options for the rear LED logo. You also get picture-in-picture for multiple input sources in an incredible variety of sizes and shapes, which seems more focused on regular work. Speaking of which… But can it handle work? Despite being very clearly focused on gaming and media, the Alienware AW3926QW makes a few concessions to working well for, well, working. That starts with the connections. In addition to HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 2.1, you get USB-C at up to 90 watts. That won’t be enough for the thirstiest gaming laptops, but most devices (including my Samsung phone) should be able to plug right in and use video and connected gadgets without a dock. You also get another USB-A port for gadgets, plus a handy array of ports on the bottom edge for quick connections: USB-C (15w), USB-A, and a headphone jack. All of this is great, and helps justify the $1100 price tag. But I think the panel is the best argument you could make for this screen as a good fit for more than gaming or movies. The RGB stripe tandem OLED panel has all the vibrant colors and perfect blacks you’d expect, but the newer RGB stripe tandem tech makes text much more legible than on my 34-inch OLED from two generations back. Between that and higher-than-typical brightness (Dell claims a peak of 1300 nits), reading text was super comfortable…aside from the glossy finish. Dell says there’s an “anti-reflective coating” on the screen, but any light in the room from a window or lamp still showed far more prominently than on any matte display. So yeah, this thing can be used for typical work, but it’s far more at home with games and movies. I won’t tell your manager (or your spouse) if you don’t. If you’re trying to justify an update purchase for an expensive monitor, this probably isn’t the most ideal one in the world…but with USB-C support and multiple inputs, including picture-in-picture, you could do a lot worse. I think you’d still be better off with, say, a 32-inch 4K OLED and a 27-inch IPS for more conventional work, but the 39-incher is undeniably cleaner and more impressive on its own. Also, I noticed some pretty dramatic “shadows” from open windows that were in the same place for a few hours. Cycling the monitor through its OLED refresh (about 8 minutes) was enough to clear them up. But if you’re worried about burn-in and you plan to use this as your primary monitor, maaaaaybe go with a cheaper option, or wait for the next generation of panels. Alienware does offer a three-year warranty against burn-in, which is comforting if you’re dropping over a grand on this. Who’s it for? If your budget will allow you to go beyond the range of 27-inch and 34-inch gaming monitors, but you lack the space for something truly enormous like the 49-inch Samsung Oddysey G9, the Alienware AW3926QW is a great choice. At just about triple the price of the excellent and affordable 27-inch Alienware AW2726DM, it makes a lot of great upgrades to justify the expense, with a brighter, sharper panel, incredible resolution, and flexible options between speed and detail. It also throws in a few premium extras like USB-C video with 90-watt charging. This monitor isn’t outstanding for more mundane tasks, as it’s hard to fit into a multi-monitor setup, and OLED burn-in might give you some real anxiety if you’re doing mostly office tasks. But if you want a single screen that does it all with a heavy focus on media, it’s definitely a good pick. And even at this price, it’s $700 below LG’s UltraGear Evo GX9, with a near-identical panel spec. I’ve already seen this monitor on sale for an even $1000, and that wasn’t even during a big sale weekend. Keep an eye on Dell’s page and you might bring that (pretty darn fair!) sticker price down a bit.

item.title: SALES: The 15 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (16 - 18 October) Pulitzer Prize-winning opera Angel's Bone arrives at the London Coliseum following its UK premiere at Manchester’s Aviva Studio in spring. The run is part of the English National Opera's dual-centre model, bringing opera to audiences in both Greater Manchester and London – with productions shaped by the venues in which they’re performed. Angel’s Bone tells the story of Mr and Mrs X.E., a desperate couple longing for a better life who discover two wounded angels in their garden. However, what begins as an act of compassion takes a darker turn, highlighting human greed and socially relevant issues. Address: London Coliseum, St Martin's Lane, London WC2N 4ES Argentine bakery Madre is the latest business to take residency in King’s Cross – and the treats are well worth making time for. The coffee shop at Fabrica X is part of The Mills Fabrica, a platform that supports innovation across techstyle and agrifood, with a focus on sustainability and social impact. Think small-batch, indulgent bites that pair fabulously well with their usual coffee offering. Address: The Mills Fabrica, 36-40 York Way, London N1 9AB A handful of new drinking dens have opened across the capital recently, just in time for cosy autumn evenings spent nursing a pint (or stronger concoction, should you so choose). The Last Exchange is the city’s newest pub, having opened its doors in Exchange Square, a stone’s throw from Liverpool Street Station. The team is determined to ‘pub properly’, with all the tipples you can imagine and a menu of elevated classics. Sip on a pint of The City Scribbler, the pub’s own house beer, and feel the stresses of city life fizzle away. Elsewhere, Bar Buah has started welcoming thirsty foodies at The White Horse, Peckham. Ex-Oranj chef Elies Salvà Ruiz de Villegas is in charge, so expect dishes such as crab caldereta and oxtail croquetas to go down very well with a glass of wine. Address: The Last Exchange, 11 Exchange Square, Broadgate, London EC2A 2BR; Bar Buah at The White Horse Peckham Website: publicanestate.com; whitehorsepeckham.co.uk 4. Have a laugh at the Leicester Square Theatre Enjoy an evening of laughs as man of many talents – comedian, writer, director and novelist among them – Andy Hamilton takes to the stage at the Leicester Square Theatre this Sunday. Cackle away as he explores the wonders and the weaknesses of human memory, touching on the nights he’ll never forget along the way. Address: Leicester Square Theatre, 6 Leicester Place, London WC2H 7BX BREW//LDN goes Bavarian for its first-ever Oktoberfest celebration this weekend, uniting 18 breweries in the same space for two days of beer-sloshing. More than 35 beers are available on tap at the site, found at Riverside East in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, plus a live oompah band, DJs and street food stalls. Address: Riverside East, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, 5 Thornton St, London E20 2AD 6. Pick up affordable pieces in Battersea Aesthetes and art lovers come together under one roof as the Affordable Art Fair Battersea returns for its autumn edition this week. The fair offers an accessible introduction to collecting with thousands of works priced under £10,000 across multiple spaces – with more than 100 galleries participating. Address: Battersea Evolution, Battersea Park, Queenstown Road, London SW11 4NJ Celebrate six years of Michelin-starred Kol, recognised as one of the best restaurants in the world, as the team throw a one-night-only celebration this Sunday. Chef and founder Santiago Lastra is transforming the restaurant into a dynamic culinary festival as four of the city’s most celebrated chefs, including Margo Henderson and Jeremy Lee, interpret iconic Mexican dishes in their own way. Tickets cost £135 per person and include a glass of biodynamic wine Gut Oggau, five dishes, and a cocktail. Address: KOL, 9 Seymour Street, London W1H 7BA 8. Experience the art of French patisserie Claridge’s Art Café has been one of London’s sleekest addresses for a sweet treat since it opened its doors. However, following a rebranding that sees Thibault Hauchard front and centre of the operation, there’s never been a better time to check out the selection on offer. Think artisan coffees, boiled eggs with truffle cheese soldiers and avo toast in the morning, before heartier lunch dishes and an array of spectacular patisserie options until close. Address: Art Café By Thibault Hauchard, Brook's Mews, London W1K 4HR 9. Find hidden treasure at a vintage market As if its array of viral street food stalls, thrift shops and various secret hideouts weren’t reason enough to visit, Camden Market welcomes a new open-air market on Saturdays this autumn in collaboration with Bootyfull Car Boot. Expect curated stalls filled with vintage fashion, retro accessories, rare vinyl records, original art and jewellery – or sell your own wares by securing a stall for £40. Address: Market Place, Hawley Wharf, NW1 10. Get soulful at Soho’s latest live music series Where better to spend an autumn evening than up high in one of the city’s glitziest rooftop bars? On select midweek nights throughout the rest of October, Flute at Broadwick Soho presents a series of live music events in collaboration with Johnnie Walker. Savour a range of limited-edition cocktails as performers including Madeleine (13 October) and Kianja (21 October) bring the soul above the colourful chaos of Soho. Address: Flute Bar, 7th floor, 20 Broadwick Street, London W1F 8TH

item.title: SALES: The 6 best cruise lines for solo travelers
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Thinking of taking a cruise as a solo traveler? Here’s the bad news: With many lines, you could end up paying twice as much as someone traveling with a companion. Most cruise ship cabins are designed for two, and the cruise rates you see advertised for these cabins are per person, based on double occupancy. That means the rates are only available to customers who will be sharing the cabin with a second paying passenger. If you want to occupy one of these cabins alone, you’ll pay a premium that, in cruise world lingo, is known as the “single supplement.” Often, that premium is 100%. In other words, even if you don’t have a second person in your cabin, you’ll be paying an extra fare as if you did. Still, all is not lost if you’re a singleton wanting to experience life at sea. Spurred by increasing demand, a growing number of cruise lines are adding cabins designed specifically for solo travelers (with pricing that, by definition, is based on single occupancy). Some lines routinely offer lower single supplement charges than others, or they reduce or waive single supplements during promotions. Others offer solo cabins sold on a guarantee basis, where you choose a cabin category but let the cruise line assign your specific room later. Of course, it’s not just a low price that makes for a good solo cruise. Just as important for many people traveling alone is the opportunity to meet other like-minded solo travelers through meet-and-greet receptions and organized group dining for solo cruisers. Some cruise lines do a better job with this than others. Looking at all these criteria — price, cabin options and a welcoming environment — I’ve identified six lines going the extra mile for cruisers traveling alone. Here are my top picks for the best cruise lines for solo travelers. Credit Norwegian Cruise Line for kicking off the trend of more solo cabins on cruise ships. In 2010, the big-ship line debuted an entire zone of small “studio” cabins for one — 128 in all — on its then-new, 4,100-passenger Norwegian Epic. It was such a hit that other lines began to follow. Just 100 square feet but superbly designed to maximize storage space, the solo rooms on Norwegian Epic are clustered around an exclusive Studio Lounge. It has a bar and television area where solo travelers can mingle at daily hosted happy hour gatherings. Norwegian has since added similar solo cabin areas with exclusive lounges to eight more ships, including its three newest vessels, Norwegian Aqua, Norwegian Viva and Norwegian Prima. Norwegian Aqua has a 93-cabin solo complex that spreads across two decks, while the somewhat smaller Norwegian Viva and Norwegian Prima both have a 73-cabin solo complex. The bigger Norwegian Encore, Norwegian Escape and Norwegian Bliss all have an 82-cabin solo complex, while two older ships — Norwegian Breakaway and Norwegian Getaway — have solo areas with 59 cabins. Norwegian also offers four solo cabins on its Hawaii-based Pride of America. Having sailed in one of Norwegian’s cabins for one on Norwegian Epic, I can confidently declare them among the coolest solo digs at sea. I particularly love the futuristic “The Jetsons”-like design and the multicolored mood lighting. One big caveat to Norwegian's solo cabins: They're mostly inside cabins without an ocean view, although they do have a window that looks out onto a corridor. On Norwegian Bliss, the solo cabins have a virtual porthole that offers a live view of the outside world via an LED screen. A bigger caveat, perhaps, is that these solo cabins have become so popular they often sell out far in advance and at prices that aren’t much better than booking a cabin for two. Royal Caribbean has taken a page from Norwegian’s playbook in recent years by adding solo cabins to both new and older ship classes. Notably, the line’s Quantum Class vessels, which began debuting in 2014, offer up to 28 of these dedicated studio cabins, which measure from 101 to 119 square feet. Unlike most of Norwegian’s solo digs, a good number of these cabins are ocean-view rooms with balconies. Others have a virtual balcony that, at first glance, looks like a veranda but is really just a digital screen projecting a real-time view of the outside. (It sounds corny, but it works.) Other Royal Caribbean ships with solo cabins include some of the line’s giant Oasis Class vessels, including Symphony of the Seas and Wonder of the Seas. Several of Royal Caribbean’s older Voyager Class and Radiance Class vessels also have solo cabins. But some of these ships have just two or three. While the solo cabins on Royal Caribbean ships don’t come with a dedicated solo lounge, solo travelers will find Royal Caribbean-hosted meetups for solo travelers on the vessels, which is a great way for single travelers to find others in the same boat, so to speak. There’s also quite a bar scene on Royal Caribbean ships, with rows of seats in many bars that are a great place to find other solo travelers. Additionally, Royal Caribbean ships are particularly known for their wide range of onboard activities, from big-production shows to rock-climbing walls and surfing pools, that you can enjoy just fine as a solo traveler. If you want to sail solo with a little old-world style, Cunard is worth a look. The line has dedicated single staterooms on three of its ships: Queen Mary 2, Queen Elizabeth and Queen Victoria. On Queen Mary 2, there are 15 of these dedicated single staterooms, while Queen Elizabeth and Queen Victoria have nine apiece — in two sizes, 150 or 180 square feet. That's a step up from the 100-square-foot studios on Norwegian Epic. Most have a large picture window and ocean views, so you won't be staring at a screen. They're on the lower decks, typically midship, a smart spot if you're prone to seasickness. As Britannia-class cabins, they come with perks that make cruising alone a little easier. You can dine solo in the Britannia Restaurant or ask to be seated with a group. Add complimentary breakfast in bed, Penhaligon's toiletries and a bottle of sparkling wine waiting on arrival, and it's a pretty civilized setup. Where Cunard really stands out is the social side. The line hosts coffee mornings and cocktail receptions for solo passengers, and on select voyages it brings aboard dance hosts who partner with passengers at evening balls. It's a throwback perk, but if you've ever wanted an excuse to spend a night in Queen Mary 2's Queens Room ballroom, this is it. Unlike Norwegian and Royal Caribbean, Silversea Cruises hasn’t created a specific cabin category for solo travelers. But the luxury line is known for catering to them with single supplements of just 10% to 25% on select sailings. Occasionally, during short-term promotions, the line even will waive the single supplement entirely. Silversea also hosts welcome receptions for solo travelers at the start of every voyage to kick off the mingling process. Operating relatively small, intimate vessels that carry just a few hundred passengers, Silversea is known for drawing a social crowd that likes to mix and mingle, particularly at dinnertime — a boon for people like me who don’t like to eat alone. Head to the main lounge just before dinner on a Silversea ship, and there’s a good chance you’ll be pulled into a conversation with a group of complete strangers who will extend a dinner invitation. This has happened to me so many times on Silversea ships that I almost count on it. On Silversea’s expedition sailings, you can also share meals with ship naturalists and expedition guides who join passengers in public dining venues. From my experience, they are always amenable to a friendly dining companion and some good conversation. Of course, there’s always the rebellious cruise line Virgin Voyages, backed by Richard Branson’s Virgin Group, which draws fun-loving folks of all ages. Each of its four ships — Scarlet Lady, Valiant Lady, Resilient Lady and Brilliant Lady — offers 46 cabins specifically designed for lone travelers. That’s a big number for ships with just 1,330 cabins overall. We haven’t yet sailed in one of these solo rooms, but based on what we saw when we toured one on Scarlet Lady, they might just be the coolest digs-for-one around. The solo accommodations on each of the Virgin Voyages ships include 40 windowless, 105-square-foot Solo Insider rooms. These sleek and stylish rooms have full-size beds, large flat-screen televisions, curvy vanities and high-design bathrooms. Six similar-looking Solo Sea View cabins on each vessel measure about 130 square feet and offer windows. Note that the solo cabins with windows are at the front of the ships, facing forward. While that’s a spectacular location for sightseeing, seasoned cruisers know that cabins in this location can be bumpy in rough seas. I love a little movement when I cruise (how else do you know you’re at sea?), but if you don’t, consider yourself warned. Meanwhile, for solos, you’ll find that Virgin’s hopping bar scene — and adults-focused atmosphere — is ideal for solos looking to meet up with other single travelers. With a ban on children under 18, you won’t find families with kids on this line. It’s all about solo travelers, couples and friend groups looking to have a good time and engage with their shipmates on board. Solo travelers looking for an upscale river cruise can often find a deal from Tauck, a high-end tour company with a European cruise division. It markets nearly a dozen river vessels. Tauck often eliminates its single supplement completely on its least-expensive category of cabins (Category 1) and reduces single supplements for other cabin categories (with savings of up to $1,000 in select categories). On board, Tauck cruise directors take special care of solo travelers, and communal tables at mealtime make it easy to meet other travelers. Cruisers traveling alone can seek out others at the bar (no worries about the bar tab — drinks are included) or escape to a quiet sundeck spot with a book when they’re tired of socializing. Daily shore excursions and tours are included, so you’ll always have a group ready to explore with you on land. River cruising is often a good choice for solo travelers, as other river lines also waive or significantly lower single supplement charges at times. Avalon Waterways waives its single supplement charge for some cabins on select cruise departures in Europe, and AmaWaterways charges a single supplement of just 25% for solo travelers booking nonsuite cabins. It also has four ships in Europe that each have two dedicated solo cabins that carry no single supplement. As someone who often cruises alone when writing about ships, I’ve found that smaller ships are often better for mixing and mingling than bigger ships, and they, thus, are a good choice for solo travelers looking to meet other people. On small ships, you’ll see the same people again and again — on tours, in lounges and around the pool. This increases the odds you’ll strike up a conversation and soon become fast friends. On big ships with thousands of passengers, you might go days without seeing the same person twice. The lines that operate small ships are also more prone to offering discounts for solo travelers, which results in a higher percentage of individual cruisers on board. That said, for the most part, the lines operating bigger ships are offering the most dedicated solo cabins. They also offer more onboard activities, from Broadway-style shows to rock-climbing walls, that you don’t need companions to enjoy. Not that you should worry too much about making friends at sea. Cruisers, in general, are social people. In fact, many passengers cruise specifically to meet others. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve been sitting alone in a corner of a cruise ship lounge, minding my own business, when another passenger (or two or five) stopped by and struck up a conversation. Whether you choose one of our top cruise lines for solo travelers or another line that suits your fancy, you’re bound to have a good time with as much or as little alone time as you desire. item.title: SALES: The best destinations to visit at Christmas for a festive escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
It’s lovely being at home at Christmas, but it is also one of our favourite times of year to travel. Seeing cities dusted in snow, with colourful fairy lights twinkling, is part of what makes the holiday season feel so special. Then there’s the plethora of festive activities on offer: from drinking mulled wine and eating gingerbread men at Christmas markets, to ice skating around a giant Christmas tree while carols play in the background. And it’s always a great time to learn more about the traditions of other cultures – did you know that in Iceland they give out books on Christmas Eve? Us neither. These are our favourite Christmas destinations. Where is the most magical place to visit at Christmas? For a truly memorable experience, you can’t go wrong with Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, the home of Santa Claus himself. Here you’ll find Santa Claus village, where you can not only meet Father Christmas (for free) but also send him your Christmas list via the Arctic Post. Where’s the best place to go away for Christmas? If you’re looking for something a little less obvious, Strasbourg in France has been dubbed the ‘Capital of Christmas’. Its title comes from the fact that it boasts the world’s largest and oldest Christmas market, totalling over 300 stalls taking over the UNESCO-listed Grande Île. The best destinations to visit at Christmas Christmas markets might feel like a modern-day invention, but the first one – The Market of the Infant Christ – actually took place over 500 years ago in Strasbourg, France. And while Germany feels like it’s the king of these markets today (Strasbourg was in German-speaking Alsace back in the 16th century) this one is still the biggest, with over 300 stalls taking over the city, selling everything from sweet treats to wooden decorations and of course, mulled wine aplenty. There’s also an ice rink by a Christmas tree at Place Kléber, plus carol concerts at the local churches too. Where to stay: You’ll be amongst the Christmas market action at the charming Hôtel Rohan Strasbourg, which is located less than a minute’s walk from the cathedral and is right by all the stalls. We have the Danish to thank for ‘hygge’, so it’s no wonder that Copenhagen feels like an especially Christmassy place to visit in December. And while it’s ideal for hunkering down and getting cosy, it’s also great for spending some time outdoors: whether that’s at the charmingly traditional fairground at Tivoli Gardens, on the ice rink at Frederiksberg Runddel, or witnessing the floating Santa Lucia kayak parade on the canals. There are also a handful of Christmas markets – the one at the colourful street of Nyhavn on the harbour is our favourite. Where to stay: Game the system and stay at Nimb Hotel, which offers its guests free and unlimited entry and rides to nearby Tivoli Gardens. Germany is known for its abundance of Christmas markets, but it is Nuremberg that holds the title for the biggest and longest-running. The scent of gingerbread fills the air as you wander the streets here, stocking up on everything from nutcrackers to Christmas ornaments, toys to confectionery. There’s even a Children’s Christmas Market, as well as a Sternenhaus, which puts on family-friendly shows and concerts. Nuremberg’s market takes itself very seriously – as it should – with strict rules on what can and cannot be sold, with only authentic, handmade pieces allowed. Be sure to try some lebkuchen (spicy, stone-baked gingerbread) and rostbratwurste drei im weggla (three small charcoal-grilled pork sausages served in a roll with mustard). Where to stay: Karl August - A Neighbourhood Hotel is a stylish bolthole in the Old Town of the city, which offers a Michelin-star restaurant and rooftop pool (it’s heated). The undisputed most Christmassy place to visit in the world is Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, the official home of Santa Claus. Located on the Arctic Circle, it’s here that you’ll find Santa Claus village, which is like stepping inside the pages of a storybook. As well as meeting Father Christmas himself, you can also visit the Post Office to send a letter to him, with a special Arctic Circle postmark. As well as having an abundance of cute activities on offer for children, there’s also a major draw for adults too: the promise of seeing the Northern Lights (but only if you’re good, of course). Where to stay: The aptly named Glass Resort is the best luxury boutique hotel in Santa Claus village, offering an atmospheric and magical place to stay with floor-to-ceiling windows and glass ceilings (natch). You could see the Northern Lights without even having to risk waking up your five-year-old. Unsurprisingly, chocolate capital Bruges is a wonderful place to spend some time at Christmas. Every year, the Winter Glow festival brings thousands of twinkly lights to the city, making it feel especially magical. As well as mainlining on chocolate, you should also sample some of the local waffles at the small Christmas market, where there’s also an ice rink. Definitely also make a pitstop at De Witte Pelikaan, a festive bauble shop, which sells hundreds of gorgeous hand-made designs for your tree. Where to stay: For the ultimate in luxury, stay at Bruges’s only five-star hotel, Hotel Dukes’ Palace. A former 15th-century ducal palace (hence the name) it boasts lavish, cosy interiors plus a great spa to warm up in after a long day spent exploring. Surrounded by snow-capped mountains, Salzburg has a real festive feel about it year-round. While its UNESCO-protected Old Town is lit up throughout December with fairy lights, and there’s a 500-year-old Christmas market and ice rink to explore, it’s the roll-call of concerts and musical performances that really stand out, with daily caroling at the Cathedral (it’s unsurprising really, as this is the birthplace of Mozart after all). Make sure you’re there for the Krampus run on 5th or 6th December if you can, when parade participants dress up in furs, bells and masks to drive off evil spirits. Where to stay: Hotel Sacher Salzburg pulls out all the stops at Christmas, with a pop-up river beach on its terrace that has an Alpine-themed bar. It’s also a short walk to the festive markets and the rest that the Old Town has to offer. Edinburgh has one of those picturesque settings that lends itself perfectly to the festive season, with narrow cobbled streets, gothic architecture, colourful houses, and, of course, a castle. Pub-hop along Princes Street and sample the best local whiskies, ice skate at St Andrew Square, or ski (yes, you read that right) at Pentland Hills Regional Park. No trip to Edinburgh at this time of year would be complete without a pitstop at The Nutcracker Christmas Shop and Ye Olde Christmas Shoppe on the Royal Mile, where you can stock up on all sorts of pressies. Where to stay: We can’t fault The Balmoral, located right next to the train station, and boasting chic tartan-infected rooms designed by Olga Polizzi. Spending time in Reykjavik during the Christmas period feels like a no-brainer. After all, it’s an inherently magical place, with its abundance of snow, geological wonders and of course, the Northern Lights. What’s more, there’s so much wonderful folklore here surrounding Christmas too: for example, from 12th December onwards, children receive presents in their shoes everyday, given to them by 13 mischievous trolls who supposedly come down from the mountains. What’s not to love? Where to stay: Minimise how much walking you need to do (read: sliding) by staying in the centre of town at the Radisson Blu 1919. Recently modernised, it’s minimalist and chic, and has happily kept a lot of the original features too, which give it a cosy charm. The Baltic city of Gdansk has a lot to offer at this time of year, not least its impressive Christmas market, which was named the best in Europe in 2024. As well as endless stalls selling homemade wares and delicious food (be sure to try zapiekanka, an open-faced toastie loaded with melted cheese, mushrooms, onions and bacon), there’s also a full programme of activities such as shows and concerts, plus a Santa’s grotto. But even if you don’t make it to the market, you can still be charmed just wandering around its storybook Old Town, with its tall, colourful buildings. Where to stay: There’s something a little Wes Anderson about the Sofitel Grand Sopot, which has a coastal location, French-inspired decor and a pastel-pink roof. You might think of Croatia as predominantly a summertime destination, with its warm climate, pebble beaches and island-hopping culture. Yet Zagreb in particular has become a hotspot for festive tourists in recent years, with much investment going into its annual Christmas market. Be sure to witness the nativity show held outside the Cathedral (complete with live animals) or one of the concerts held on the balconies of the city. Where to stay: The five-star Esplanade Zagreb Hotel is the city’s most iconic hotel. Originally built in 1925 to welcome passengers arriving from the Orient Express, it still has that Old World glamour, with spacious rooms and Art Deco flourishes, not to mention one of the best restaurants for traditional Croatian cuisine in town, Le Bistro. As the Catholic heartland of Europe, it’s unsurprising that Rome feels especially festive. It’s a wonderful time to visit the Vatican, where you can see the Christmas tree being lit in front of St. Peter’s Basilica, attend Christmas Eve Midnight Mass, or witness the Pope’s traditional Urbi et Orbi blessing. There’s also something particularly magical about seeing the ancient sites – such as the Coliseum and the Pantheon – surrounded by twinkly fairy lights, and what’s more comforting at this time of year than a hearty bowl of pasta? Where to stay: To be close to all the city’s attractions, check in to Hotel Eden, Dorchester Collection – if it’s good enough for Naomi Campbell, it’s good enough for us.

item.title: SALES: The Best Airbnbs in Amsterdam, From Canal Houses to a Boat on the Amstel River

Amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century. To a history-loving teenager visiting Europe for the first time, the Dutch capital was a wonderland of Van Goghs. It felt so different from my hometown, yet still approachable, and sparked my lifelong love of travel. What has changed since then is the crowds. Amsterdam is now one of Europe's most visited cities, so you'll need to book tickets to the major sites well in advance, especially during summer. The same goes for accommodations. On more than a dozen return trips (many by train from Belgium, where I used to live), I have stayed everywhere from youth hostels to boutique hotels to Airbnbs. And over the years, I've learned that renting an Airbnb offers a completely different way to experience the city. Whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way. Read on for a few of my favorite Airbnbs in Amsterdam, whether you're here for the art, the nightlife, or to explore by bike. Our top picks: FAQ: What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Amsterdam? Book a stay in the Grachtengordel (canal ring) for the quintessential Amsterdam experience. The Jordaan has a similarly atmospheric feel with slightly quieter surroundings, while the Museum District puts the city's famous art museums right at your doorstep. item.title: SALES: Help Papa Johns Rate Your Order With AI and You Could Get a Free Pizza
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Influencers aren't the only ones being rewarded for snapping photos of their food. Papa Johns is running a promotion that's handing out free pizza in exchange for pics of your most recent order. The pizza chain wants to examine the images for quality-control purposes. "Every photo and every review helps us better understand what customers love and where we can improve as we continue our journey to deliver a better experience every time they choose Papa Johns," says Chris Lyn-Sue, Global Chief Marketing Officer at Papa Johns. The company's press release doesn't mention AI, but CEO Todd Penegor told Reuters that uploaded images will be analyzed by AI via a system it created with Google Cloud. Papa Johns has in-store cameras that do something similar, but they're only in a few hundred of its approximately 6,000 stores, Reuters says.
So, it's looking to supplement those pics with customer images. Plus, it'll help Papa Johns keep an eye on potential inconsistencies across franchises, the "Achilles heel" of the fast-food brand, Penegor told Reuters.

The company makes some bold claims about its accuracy, including better mixed and AI-polished content identification and a false-positive rate of just 1 in 10,402. That’s impressive if true. So, to test out those claims, and to see how GPTZero compares to other top detectors, I put it through my own battery of tests. GPTZero in brief: - Price: Free up to 10,000 words per month; Premium: $12.99/month; Professional: $24.99/month (billed annually) - Supported languages: 26 total languages (including English) - File uploads/formats: PDF, .docx, .txt, and image files - AI models it claims to detect: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Grok, DeepSeek, and others - Company: GPTZero Inc., based in New York, United States What features does GPTZero offer? GPTZero uses a deep-learning model trained on human-written and AI-generated text to determine if a text was written by an AI, human, or a combination of the two. You can either paste text directly into the dashboard or upload a document for analysis. Once the scan is complete, GPTZero provides an AI probability score, a confidence rating, and a sentence-by-sentence breakdown of the results. With its latest model, GPTZero also tries to distinguish between human writing that’s been polished with AI, entirely AI-generated content, and AI text that’s been rewritten using a paraphrasing tool. This is the trickiest part of AI-detection and mixed text is often what is most open to interpretation by these services. After pasting or uploading text, GPTZero offers an Advanced Scan feature that highlights the passages most responsible for a document’s overall classification. There’s also an AI Patterns tool that looks for common characteristics of AI writing, such as repeatedly grouping ideas into threes, and explains why those patterns might be suspicious. This extra level of detail and transparency about its detection results is admirable, and not something most competitors display. Seeing why a detector reached a particular conclusion rather than just a flat score is really helpful when combing back through the text yourself. GPTZero handles text that isn’t black or white a bit differently. The company says it generally leans toward marking text as human-written when it isn’t confident enough to flag as AI-written. That’s an understandable way to reduce false positives, but it also means theoretically, some AI-generated content could go undetected. Just because GPTZero classifies something as human-written doesn’t mean it’s guaranteed to be free of AI content—again, another reason I recommend using detectors as a guide, and always double-checking the text yourself. Outside of its detection tools, GPTZero has a few other useful features. It supports batch file uploads and downloadable reports, although the limits vary depending on your subscription. There’s also a Chrome extension that lets you scan text directly from webpages without having to copy and paste it into the dashboard. The extension works with Google Docs as well, where GPTZero’s Writing Replay feature tracks a document’s editing history, including typing and pasting activity. While some might find this unnecessarily intrusive, it can be a really intriguing feature because it lets you see how a document came together instead of relying entirely on an AI detector’s prediction. GPTZero also includes a separate plagiarism checker that matches text with existing sources and provides references to any original documents that may have been copied. There’s also a Hallucination Check feature that looks for potentially AI-hallucinated reference sources and poorly supported claims. I wouldn’t call it a full-fledged fact-checker, but it helps maintain a certain level of academic integrity. Finally, GPTZero offers a few integrations aimed at schools, businesses, and developers. These include Canvas and Google Classroom support, a Microsoft Word add-in, and an API for incorporating GPTZero’s detection tools into other software. How much does GPTZero cost? GPTZero offers a free plan and two paid plans: Premium and Professional. The Free plan lets you scan up to 10,000 words per month and includes basic AI detection, one Advanced Scan, and five AI highlighting sessions through its Chrome extension. It’s a fine starting point if you only need to check the occasional article or essay, but the limited access to GPTZero’s more advanced analysis tools can leave you wanting more—I guess that’s the point though. Premium costs $23.99 per month, or $12.99 per month when billed annually—$155.88 for the year. It includes 300,000 words per month, unlimited Advanced Scans, downloadable AI reports, and a 50,000-character limit per scan. Professional costs $45.99 per month, or $24.99 per month when billed annually—$299.88 for the year. You’ll get a monthly allowance of 500,000 words and a per-scan limit increase to 150,000 characters. It also supports batches of up to 250 files and adds features for businesses such as Learning Management System (LMS) integration. Using Premium’s full 300,000-word allowance works out to about $4.33 per 100,000 words with annual billing, or $8 with monthly billing. That is a little bit cheaper than competitors on an annual basis, but a bit more expensive when paying month-to-month. I recommend trying out the free plan first to determine your usage frequency and needs. If you need the Advanced Scan breakdown data, or you use the service a lot, then Premium is the way to go. While the annual discount is substantial, it won’t be much of a bargain for a tool if you rarely use it. How well does GPTZero detect AI-generated text? To test GPTZero, I ran 50 different text samples through the detector. These covered five categories: 100 percent human-written, 100 percent AI-generated, human writing edited by AI, AI-generated text edited by a human, and mixed documents containing roughly equal amounts of both. GPTZero correctly identified every purely human-written and AI-generated sample I tested, including text from every major LLM model. Things became a little less precise with edited texts. GPTZero classified two AI-written but human-edited samples as overwhelmingly human-written, despite most of their content originating from AI. It also struggled a bit to consistently recognize when AI had been used to edit human writing. GPTZero performed much better with mixed documents containing entire sections of AI-generated text alongside human writing. It caught the AI involvement in all 10 mixed samples. Overall, I’d say that GPTZero excels at detecting unedited AI-generated text and performs well with mixed documents. But GPTZero can be fooled if someone takes AI-generated writing and substantially edits or rewrites it. Still, it was a good showing and the results rank at the top compared to competitors. How well does GPTZero detect pure AI text? GPTZero had no trouble spotting purely AI-generated text in my tests. I ran 10 entirely AI-generated sample texts through the detector, a mixture from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok. It flagged all of them as 100 percent AI-generated, giving it a perfect detection rate in this category. It doesn’t get any better than that, particularly since the samples came from four different chatbots. It also performed well in my repeatability test. I ran the same sample text three times through GPTZero and every time it returned the same 100 percent AI score. Of course, 10 samples are a relatively small test pool, and a 100 percent AI score doesn’t definitively prove that a chatbot wrote something. But based on my results there’s no arguing that GPTZero is pretty dang good at catching fully generated AI text, no matter the AI model you use. Does GPTZero mistake human writing for AI? GPTZero was equally impressive at recognizing human-written text. I tested another 10 samples, this time written entirely by humans, and it correctly identified every one as 100 percent human and 0 percent AI. That’s a perfect detection rate in this category. Again, it was consistent as well. I ran the same human-written sample through the detector three times, and GPTZero returned an identical 0 percent AI score each time. False positives—when human writing is incorrectly labeled as AI written—can have serious consequences. Nobody wants their work wrongly flagged as AI-generated, especially if it leads to accusations of cheating at school or issues at work. The samples I used included writing from myself, colleagues, and friends, each with a unique writing style. Despite these differences, GPTZero didn’t produce a single false positive. This is encouraging and leads me to trust the company’s claimed 1 in 10,402 false-positive rating. Can editing AI text fool GPTZero? This is the kind of writing that most often throws AI detectors for a loop. And the same can be said about GPTZero—for the most part, at least. I tested 10 samples that were originally AI-generated but that I had substantially edited myself. As a whole, all were still roughly 75 percent AI-written, yet GPTZero classified one as 96 percent human and the other as 98 percent human. It did flag one of the samples as AI-polished, but otherwise missed most of the AI involvement. I also tested 10 human-written samples that had been edited with AI so they resulted in roughly 75 percent human-written and 25 percent AI-written. GPTZero estimated that one was 24 percent AI-generated, which is remarkably accurate, and classified another as 100 percent human, which is at least in the ballpark. So it picked up on some AI involvement, but the results were a tad inconsistent. GPTZero did much better when I tested documents containing separate sections of AI- and human-written text—GPTZero calls them “Mixed.” I ran 10 samples through the detector, each with a roughly 50/50 split between human- and AI-written. GPTZero returned AI scores of 74, 50, 64, 58, and 54 percent, and flagged one as AI-polished—technically incorrect, but I’ll give it points for recognizing the AI-written content. While not perfect, that’s a much better showing. GPTZero picked up on AI involvement in all samples, even if the scores varied a bit. For what it’s worth, GPTZero states that these percentages are detection scores, not measurements of how much of the text was actually written by AI. So what can we take away from this showing? GPTZero seems pretty good at spotting chunks of AI-generated writing mixed into human text. But when someone takes AI-generated content and heavily edits it themself, the detector has a much harder time. This is more of an issue with all AI detectors rather than GPTZero in particular. They all struggle with heavily human-edited AI text. How does GPTZero handle privacy and data? It might not always cross your mind, but privacy is a big deal with AI detectors. This is especially true if you’re uploading sensitive or confidential documents. According to GPTZero, text submitted through its website dashboard is stored only so users can access their scan history. It says it doesn’t train its detection models on submissions from paid users, teachers, or institutional customers. Free users’ submissions, on the other hand, are not exempt from this data collection and their data may be anonymized and used to improve the detector. Users can also delete their scan history, and GPTZero says that deleted submissions are excluded from future model training. For API users, submitted text isn’t stored at all nor used to improve GPTZero’s products. Privacy-conscious users can feel reassured by this. Still, I’d be careful uploading sensitive documents, since dashboard submissions are stored on GPTZero’s servers unless you delete them yourself. GPTZero’s privacy policy also addresses how long it keeps the personal information of its users. The company retains it only as long as necessary, usually no more than three months after an account is closed, with exceptions for legal issues and niche backup purposes. Depending on their region, users can also request access or deletion of their personal information. Writing Replay is also worth scrutinizing before you enable it. The browser extension records editing activity on supported pages and sends that information to GPTZero’s servers. Users can turn off recording and delete individual replays from the dashboard, but disabling the feature won’t erase anything already recorded. On the security front, GPTZero reports SOC 2 Type II compliance and says its privacy practices are designed to meet GDPR and CCPA requirements. Those are encouraging signs, although specifics about how individual features collect and retain information are not detailed. Overall, I wouldn’t worry too much about uploading everyday, nonsensitive writing into GPTZero. But if I were working with confidential documents, I’d weigh whether it was worth it. At the very least, you should always store your documents somewhere else and make sure to delete them from GPTZero’s dashboard as soon as you’re finished. Is GPTZero worth it? GPTZero is one of the better AI detectors I’ve tested. It had no trouble identifying purely human-written and AI-generated text, and I didn’t encounter a single false positive in my tests. It also did a good job with mixed content, although it struggled more when AI-generated writing had been heavily edited. Accuracy aside, there’s plenty else to like here. The interface is clean and easy to navigate, the analysis tools offer a plethora of detail, and extras such as plagiarism checking and Writing Replay are genuinely useful. The free version is absolutely worth trying if you only need to check the occasional document, while heavy users should opt for the Premium plan instead. Although par for the course with AI detectors, users should still recognize that GPTZero has difficulties handling heavily edited AI text. Also, its data retention practices might concern ultra privacy-conscious users. GPTZero gets a lot right though, and I think it’s one of the best services around, especially for educators and writers thanks to its extra tools. Editor’s note: Because online services are often iterative, gaining new features and performance improvements over time, this review is subject to change in order to accurately reflect the current state of the service. Any changes to text or our final review verdict will be noted at the top of this article.

item.title: SALES: The Best Places to Go in Africa in 2027
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
While editing this year’s list, one thing quickly became very clear: 2027 is poised to be a banner one for cultural experiences across Africa. While chatting with our writers, I kept finding compelling reasons to go back to my favorite corners—the Kigali Triennale’s return to Rwanda in February, Jazzablanca’s 20th anniversary in Casablanca, and an even more vibrant creative landscape in Tunis than the one I reported on six years ago. But now I’m adding Benin to my list, thanks to four—yes, four—eagerly anticipated new museums debuting in the year ahead that will showcase everything from modern art to critical artifacts recently repatriated from Europe. Elsewhere on the continent there are fresh ways to experience some of its familiar pleasures, owing to a high-end resort boom on the beaches of Zanzibar, a host of safari lodge openings in Zambia, eight new marine reserves in São Tomé and Principe, and a groundbreaking five-country trans-frontier conservation area. Be sure to make some time for rarer incentives to travel too, like a once-in-a-generation “superbloom” in South Africa and the “eclipse of the century” over Luxor, Egypt (it also helps that there are some swish new places to stay at these places).But one of the most endearing stories of an African destination of the past year may be Cape Verde: Is the “World Cup effect” going to bring a wave of curious travelers to the archipelago? Read on to decide for yourself. —Sarah Khan This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here. Go for: a museum boom and a vibrant cultural milieu Benin is a place where history runs deep: It’s home to the ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, the spiritual traditions of Vodun, and Ouidah—one of West Africa’s significant ports in the transatlantic slave trade. Now the country is turning that history into a new era of cultural tourism, while creating ways for travelers, particularly people of African descent, to reconnect with their heritage. Ouidah, an especially important destination for those tracing their ancestry, is central to that effort. In 2025 the government announced plans to invest $1.4 billion in tourism and cultural development, including for infrastructure, heritage restitution, and indigenous traditions. In 2027 that transformation is expected to become more visible with a host of new museum openings, like the Museum of Modern Art in Cotonou; the International Museum of Memory and Slavery in Ouidah; and the Museum of the Epic of the Amazons and Kings of Dahomey in Abomey. The latter of which is expected to house 26 royal artifacts repatriated by France in 2021. Vodun Days, an eight-day celebration of Benin’s indigenous spiritual traditions taking place January 2–9, 2027, will showcase ceremonies, music, and dance. Meanwhile, Villa Karo in Grand-Popo—a bridge between artists and researchers from Finland, Sweden, and West Africa—will continue its residency program, which brings artists to its seaside research center to connect with the local community through workshops, concerts, and exhibitions. The famous stilt village of Ganvié, meanwhile, remains open to visitors as its Reinventing the Lakeside City of Ganvié project upgrades tourism infrastructure. Benin is also beginning to make appearances on cruise itineraries. Two new Swan Hellenic sailings in 2027 sailings feature the country, including an April voyage from Luanda to Accra and an October sailing from Ghana to Angola. —Harriet Akinyi Go for: beaches, festivals, and new-found buzz During FIFA World Cup 2026, one of the most impressive performances came from Cape Verde, an archipelago of 10 islands off Africa’s Atlantic Ocean coast. Now the “World Cup effect” has gotten travelers curious about what the destination has to offer. It helps that getting there is easier than ever, thanks to new direct flights launched in May 2026 from Rhode Island’s T.F. Green International Airport on Cabo Verde Airlines. On the island of Sal, which boasts white-sand beaches and over 350 days of sunshine a year, adrenaline-driving activities range from swimming with lemon sharks to kite- and windsurfing, while those seeking a more relaxed experience can float in the saline pools of Pedra de Lume. The island’s luxury accommodation options are also getting an upgrade with Hyatt Regency Cape Verde Sal as well as a family-friendly all-inclusive Bahia Principe set to open in 2027. In March the 322-room Robinson Boa Vista will welcome its first guests to the easternmost island of Boa Vista, known as the Sahara in the Atlantic due to its desert-like flat plains. São Vicente and Praia are the islands to hit for local music—the samba-inspired São Vicente Carnival features dance performances, fireworks, and floats, while Praia hosts the annual Kriol Jazz Festival and the Atlantic Music Expo. Africa’s first Four Points by Sheraton resort opened in the port city of São Vicente last March, with 105 rooms and 22 suites overlooking either Laginha Beach, known for its turquoise waters, or the Monte Verde mountains. —Mazuba Kapambwe Go for: a vibrant cultural and design scene Casablanca stealthily enters 2027 as Africa’s most creative urban reinvention. It’s an apt year to visit, given the pioneering Royal Air Maroc flights, launched in June 2026, linking Casablanca with Los Angeles—the first African connection to America's Pacific Coast. It is a poetic bridge, connecting the dream factory that conjured Casablanca’s mythic character with the modern metropolis redefining itself as a vanguard of contemporary Maghrebi culture. A cornerstone of this cultural renaissance is the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July: Once an intimate gathering, it has evolved into North Africa's best boutique music festival, hosting emerging Afrobeat, jazz, and urban artists beneath the modernist skyscrapers in Anfa Park and on stages in the palm-lined Arab League Park beside the Nevada skate park. Design lovers, meanwhile, can admire the Museum of Photography and Visual Arts, which was inaugurated in June in the medina and is Tadao Ando’s sole architectural project on the continent. The museum and the recently launched annual Morocco Design fair, which spotlights high-end design studios, establish Casablanca as an emerging destination for cutting-edge design, music, and art. The city's heritage sites are getting a revamp too. The iconic 1916 Neo-Moorish Lincoln Hotel by Radisson Collection is being masterfully revived by French Moroccan architects OUALALOU + CHOI, who are pairing its historic façade with an über-minimalist interior. From the hotel’s doorstep, a new tramline whisks you to the Casablanca Finance City (CFC), a glittering new commercial district composed of futuristic, climate-resilient buildings that pay homage to Casablanca’s legacy of concrete experimentation. Nearby, bougie restaurants like Le 7ème Ciel draw crowds and a new Radisson Red will open in 2027 to join an existing Radisson Blu. CFC is built on the old Anfa Airport, from which The Little Prince author and architecture school dropout Antoine de Saint-Exupéry flew a perilous mail route to Dakar in an open-cockpit Bréguet 14 biplane, returned for drinks at Le Petit Poucet, and lived with his fiery Salvadorean muse, Consuelo Suncín. Then, as now, the city was a nexus connecting continents and a frontier to the future. —Paula Hardy Go for: a ground-breaking cross-border safari project and birding adventure In a world where ecological degradation and global discord are reasons to despair, Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is more rising sun than ray of hope. Supported by five countries—Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, the world’s largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area encompasses a region roughly the size of France and is watered by the Kavango, Zambezi, Chobe, Kwando, and Kafue river systems. Officially launched in 2012, it languished as a plan on paper for years, but recent initiatives have seen it shake off bureaucratic paralysis: Green Growth for KAZA, the umbrella initiative, directly links community benefits to conservation. Several depleted parks have been rewilded; Africa’s first cross-border avitourism project, the Great Kavango Zambezi Birding Route, was recently launched; and connectivity improved—Shearzone Safari launched a charter service in Zambia in early 2026. Notably, Angola has entered the guided-safari arena with Luiana Plains Expedition Camp, the first to open in the 10.3-million-acre Luengue-Luiana National Park in July 2026. It will soon be followed by Natural Selection, which is developing a new 500,000-acre game reserve around Angola’s existing Cuatir Reserve. In Namibia’s unsung Zambezi Region, Thitake River Lodge opens on the banks of the Kwando in Bwabwara National Park late in 2026, while Nkasa Linyanti is the fabulous new linchpin in Nkasa Rupara National Park. But the KAZA TFCA region that’s experiencing the biggest proliferation is Zambia, buoyed by the scrapping of visa requirements of 53 countries and increased international flights. Ker & Downey launched its Zambia division with King Lewanika Lodge in remote Liuwa Plains National Park, the first luxury base from which to witness Africa’s second-largest wildebeest migration; its second location, Musesenji River Camp, opens in April 2027. And luring the well-heeled to 5.5-million-acre Kafue National Park are Anantara with Tented Camp Kafue River, and Classic Zambia with new Lwenge River Camp; both opened this summer. —Pippa de Bruyn Go for: a wave of gallery and festival openings turning a gorilla trek stopover into an art capital For years Kigali has been seen as little more than a pit stop before going gorilla trekking. Now the city is making a compelling case for staying awhile. The city’s vibrant food and fashion have already been putting it on the map, and now the art scene is getting noticed as several institutions build platforms for championing Rwandan and East African artists. February 2027 marks the second edition of the Kigali Triennial, which is primed to rival some of the continent’s more established art festivals, like ART X Lagos and Dak'Art Biennale. The Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art, which opened at the end of 2025, highlights artists across East Africa with two exhibitions: “Space Encounters,” exploring human connection and memory, which is currently on through December 2026; and a collection of contemporary work by Sudanese artists opening in January 2027. This follows the debut of the Inyuguti Art Hub this year, which brought together 19 artists from across Africa and the UK, including Rwandan Elisa Niyogisubizo (also the gallery’s founder), Burundi-based Peter Kamale, and Nigerian Pascal Ejiofor. The lines between the art and hotel scenes are beginning to blur too, with a new generation of properties doubling as cultural showcases. Among them is the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members club that opened in early 2026 as Rwanda’s first women-led ultraluxury boutique property, showcasing the owner’s private art collection. Creative events are rippling beyond the capital, as Rwandan artists Willy Karekezi and Cedric Mizero are each launching new spaces in Musanze, the gateway town for gorilla trekking, in 2027: Karekezi will open a residency alongside his Indiba Arts Space in Kigali, and Mizero will open Umugenzi, an addition to the multisite Ikinyugunyugu art residency. —Vivienne Dovi Go for: the eclipse of the century and nostalgia-soaked Nile cruises Dubbed the eclipse of the century, 2027’s much-anticipated celestial event will reach its zenith in Luxor, Egypt, on August 2, when the moon will block out the sun for a record-breaking 6 minutes and 23 seconds. Fitting, perhaps, for a place where the mystical has always loomed large, the mountains hold secret treasures, the temples and tombs have been perfectly preserved roughly 3,000 years after they were built, and the Nile exudes a life force of its own. Travelers have come to this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, nearly 400 miles south of Cairo, for millennia. Luxor itself served as Egypt’s capital from 1570 BCE to 1069 BCE, but today is better known as the home of the Valley of the Kings, and the start or end point of nostalgia-infused Nile cruises to and from Aswan, a leisurely four- or five-day sail away. Both destinations are primed for a momentous 2027: In Luxor the much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter’s base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery—will reopen in July as a Mandarin Oriental after an extensive renovation exactly 120 years after its official inauguration. Aswan’s own grande dame, the Old Cataract, which famously inspired Agatha Christie’s best-selling novel Death on the Nile, has also been taken over by Mandarin Oriental and will reopen its Nile Wing in 2027 after a thorough upgrade. Mandarin Oriental will launch its first Nile cruise that connects the two, joining a flurry of other new boats taking to the ancient waterway. Among them Oberoi’s Melouk and Malekat dahabiyas, with only seven cabins apiece, and homegrown operator Kemetale’s second boat, Deshret, with its Nile-view sauna, plunge pool, and spa treatments. —Selina Denman Go for: a rare ‘superbloom’ of endemic flora and world-class wines at Africa’s southern tip. Cape Town. Winelands. Then head off on safari. That’s the typical circuit for travelers jetting into South Africa. But in 2027 look beyond to the Overberg—“over mountain” in Afrikaans—region, where wildfires have triggered a floral extravaganza not seen in decades. Base yourself in Hermanus for memorable whale watching from the seven-and-a-half-mile Cliff Path. The Marine Hotel, a seafront landmark since 1902, has unveiled a fynbos-inspired revamp of its public spaces and seafood-driven Pavilion Restaurant. There’s a new culinary energy in town too: Chef Michael Broughton, previously at Terroir in Stellenbosch, has turned the historic Fisherman’s Cottage into a hotbed of polished Cape coastal cuisine (don’t miss the spaghetti aglio e olio with local rock lobster). Broughton’s wine list leans into estates from the nearby Hemel-en-Aarde (Heaven and Earth) valley, where cellars are known for exceptional Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Creation Wines offers a new sculpture-led vineyard walk, and opens a private tasting room in May 2027 aimed at wine lovers looking for a deep dive into the cool-climate terroir. Bouchard Finlayson, one of the oldest estates in the valley, reopens in late 2027 after an extensive renovation, with a new tasting space and art collection. Set in the heart of the Cape Floristic Region, Grootbos Private Nature Reserve is a biodiversity hot spot. Wildfires that swept the area in 2025 sparked a superbloom of new growth, including dormant species that haven’t flowered in decades like wild orchids and the fire-dependent Gladiolus overbergensis. Guided botanical walks and drives get you in the thick of the fynbos, but a new equestrian center also makes this a great choice for horse-riding holidays. Long popular with families, Coot Club, on the nearby Klein River Lagoon, expands in 2027 with a pair of new two-bedroom boathouses and brings a new wellness focus with outdoor yoga sessions and in-room wellness treatments. Toast it all with a sundowner in the refreshed Flamingo Bar upstairs in the original homestead. An hour’s drive east, Cape Agulhas, the southernmost tip of Africa, is a fitting finale. A new interpretation center delves into the history and geology of Agulhas, after which you can climb the 177-year-old lighthouse and stand on the rocky shoreline where the Indian and Atlantic Oceans meet. —Richard Holmes Go for: new marine reserves and World Heritage Sites On the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, more than 155 miles off the coast of Gabon in the Gulf of Guinea, a thick rainforest punctuated by needle-like rock formations meets shores of white and volcanic black sand. One of the world’s least visited countries, and known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, this island nation is surrounded by clear turquoise waters brimming with manta rays and reef and nurse sharks. Humpback whales migrate through seasonally, and turtles begin to nest on the beaches in November before hatching between February and April. In 2025 the first two of eight new dedicated marine reserves, Santana and Ilhéu das Rolas, were approved; in 2026, six roças, or former Portuguese plantations, were designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites, recognized for their role in shaping the social, economic, and cultural history of the nation, which was once the world’s preeminent supplier of cacao. Two of these roças are a part of the Príncipe Collection—the hospitality arm of sustainable development group HBD Príncipe—meaning you can stay at these historically significant sites. One of the properties on offer is Hotel Belo Monte, which opened in June and sits high up on a hillside overlooking the rainforest and sea. A stay in this eco-hideaway, chicly styled with splashes of bold color, comes with cultural insight and an immersion into the wild surroundings. Another outpost, Sundy Praia, is set within what was once part of Príncipe’s second-largest cocoa plantation on the remote northwest tip and hosts guests in tented villas backing the golden shores on the remote northwest tip of the island. —Lauren Jade Hill Go for: ancient treasures and contemporary culture by the sea Designated 2027’s Arab Capital of Tourism, this languid North African city now pulses with the energy of a new generation of Tunisian creatives and entrepreneurs. Events planned in the historic Medina range from TedX Pasha Street talks and musical retreats to artisanal workshops, many organized by the beloved Dar Ben Gacem boutique hotel and cultural hub, which will also host a rooftop event for August’s solar eclipse. Across the Medina, near the Great Mosque of Zitouna, Dar Ben Turkia's early 2026 opening expands the luxury-hotel options that preserve the area’s history. The elegant eight-suite hideaway has an in-house hammam and spa, so it doubles as a wellness retreat in the heart of the Medina. Beyond the medieval city’s labyrinths, the sun-kissed ruins of ancient Carthage spill toward the coast. Anchoring these archaeological riches is the Carthage National Museum, slated to reopen by year-end after an eight-year overhaul. For more contemporary treasures, head downhill to the city’s leading art gallery, Selma Feriani, which in 2027 will exhibit major Tunisian artists Mohamed Amine Hamouda and Rafik El Kamel. Nearby, sleek seaside city La Marsa gives way to the historically working-class neighborhood of Bhar Lazreg, where artists and makers have been repurposing spaces. Anchors like the B7L9 Art Centre (built by and for the area’s community), and Phosphor Creative District—showcasing local talent who specialize in everything from fine art to design—are transforming the area into a meeting place for artists, demonstrating why the neighborhood has become known as one of Tunis’s coolest. Meanwhile, fashionable La Marsa remains a firm favorite with the stylish set, and mid-2026 restaurant openings like Oto, a Japanese izakaya, and Sujet, a hybrid café and design store, keep things fresh. When you’re ready for a break, make your way up the coast to Birdie at The Clubhouse in Gammarth, which opened in August 2026, or south to Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that began welcoming guests in September. Perched on the forested edge of the iconic blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, this whitewashed six-room sanctuary with sweeping Mediterranean views feels almost untouched by time. —Lee Middleton Go for: a host of new hotels from which to experience some of Africa’s best beaches Most visitors arrive in Zanzibar with postcard perfection already in mind—turquoise shallows, swaying palms, and dhows tipping into the sunset—but the island’s enduring drawcard is still Stone Town: a UNESCO-listed tangle of coral-rag limestone alleys, carved Omani doors, and clove-scented air, where Africa, Arabia, and India have intersected for centuries. In 2027 Zanzibar gets its most serious branded hotel wave yet with the 181-key Anantara Zanzibar Resort & Residences on the north coast, and in 2028 it will welcome, the 60-villa Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe, widely regarded as the loveliest beach on the east coast. The latter is a short flight from the brand’s Serengeti lodge and has been built with a bush-and-beach pairing in mind. The freshest energy is homegrown, though, and it has moved away from the overdeveloped north. In Jambiani, on the sunrise-facing southeast coast, the seven-villa Ma’a Salama (“go in peace”) opened in mid-2026 as a nonprofit that doubles as a hospitality school, training island youth in exchange for a year’s free education. Ma’a Salama’s spacious villas are named for spices and are cooled by bioclimatic design rather than air-conditioning, and four are crowned with rooftop teahouses, designed in Stone Town’s famous Emerson’s teahouses. On the quiet southwest coast at Kizimkazi, Kizikula is the antithesis of a resort: no sign, no jetty, just a jungly pathway leading to what feels more like a private home or artist’s enclave than a hotel. At low tide, guests access the beach through a secret gap in the coral cliff. Designed by Mumbai’s Case Design, its coral-limestone rooms sit in wild permaculture gardens. In 2026 the resort added 19 rooms, and in December it will open a new rooftop sunset bar and a three-floor wellness center, where treatments incorporate ingredients like Zanzibari cinnamon, turmeric, and cardamom. As of October 2026 Airlink flies the first-ever nonstop route between Cape Town and Zanzibar, with low-cost FlySafair rumored to be expanding its regular Johannesburg service to include Cape Town too. The UK gets its own first direct link in November 2027, courtesy of TUI Airways’s Gatwick service, along with a direct London flight from Air Tanzania. —Jane Broughton
